title: Record elective surgeries show things could be looking up for Canberra's health system
text:
The ACT's health portfolio is changing hands for the first time in seven years, with new minister Marisa Paterson inheriting a sector plagued by chronically long surgery waiting lists.

However, the latest elective surgery figures indicate the situation may be improving.

While waiting lists are indeed "still long", a record number of elective surgeries were performed at Canberra hospitals in 2025-26.

Nearly 18,000 elective surgeries were completed last financial year — a new record for the system, and an increase of 1,000 surgeries on the previous financial year.

About 30 per cent of those were for patients from outside the ACT, in the surrounding region.

“We've gone from just over 2,000 patients being overdue last year to just over 1,000 now,” Dr Gert Frahm-Jensen, Canberra Hospital's clinical surgery director, said.

" And so we've not only caught up on the elective operations that have come in through the year, we've also managed to reduce the long waits of yesteryear. "

But while the number of patients waiting longer than clinically recommended for their surgery reduced, there are still more than 1,000 patients on the books who are overdue for elective surgery.

Dr Gert Frahm-Jensen, clinical director of surgery at Canberra Hospital, says they've "caught up" on some of the elective surgery backlog. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

Record number of elective surgeries

The data, released to the ABC yesterday, shows that, as of June 30 this year, 17,569 patients who were on elective surgery waiting lists had their surgeries done.

That figure is an increase of 6 per cent — or 1,000 surgeries — on 2024-2025's figures.

Hundreds waiting for orthopaedic surgery in Canberra After 36 years working as a house cleaner, Judy Harman needs a knee replacement, but there are 200 people in front of her on the wait list for orthopaedic surgery in Canberra.

That improvement is attributed to better patient flow through the new Centralised Operations Centre, and the $100 million government investment in increasing elective surgery capacity.

Canberra Health Services (CHS) chief operating officer Alison Derrett confirmed there were still 1,274 people overdue for their elective surgery — which is a 37 per cent decrease on the previous year — but said CHS had been working hard to prioritise category one patients that were meant to have their surgery within 30 days.

"Back in January we had about 100 of those patients, and at the end of June we were right down to 14 of those patients," she said.

" So we will continue to really target people in their category time frame for surgery. "

At the end of June, nearly 40 category two patients who should have had surgery within 90 days, had been on the waitlist for more than a year.

Chief operating officer Alison Derrett says Canberra Health Services has been working hard to prioritise category one patients that were meant to have their surgery within 30 days. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

While health is the ACT government's biggest spend — making up around a third of the annual budget — CHS has had difficulty attracting specialists to the capital, which they've cited as one reason for the long elective surgery wait times for ACT patients.

Emergency department wait times in the ACT have also consistently been longer than the national average.

On her final day as health minister, Rachel Stephen-Smith acknowledged that while "waiting lists are still long," she was confident the health sector was "in a really good place".

"We've significantly improved emergency department performance," she said.

"We've done a record number of … elective surgeries and are starting to really get that elective surgery waiting list and waiting times down.

" There's never going to be a time in the health portfolio where there aren't a lot of challenges, but we have a very clear path forward. "

ACT Deputy Chief Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith has retained the health infrastructure portfolio despite handing over the health and mental health ministries. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

'Up for the challenge'

On the whole, the figures would be welcome news for incoming health minister Marisa Paterson.

For the first time in seven years, the ACT's health portfolio has changed hands, as part of the Labor cabinet reshuffle sparked by the resignation of then-deputy chief and education minister Yvette Berry last week.

Ms Paterson told ABC Radio Canberra that she was "absolutely over the moon" to be appointed health minister, and that she had put herself forward for the role.

"It is a very important portfolio that matters to Canberrans, and I think it's a great challenge, and I'm really up for the challenge," she said.

She said she was eager to continue the "significant work" Ms Stephen-Smith had done.

"A key pressing issue for the government is obviously the enterprise bargaining negotiations that are currently underway," Ms Paterson said.

Incoming ACT health minister Marisa Paterson says she is eager to continue the significant work started by her predecessor. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

"I'll work very closely with the unions and with Minister Stephen-Smith to work towards a positive outcome there.

" But ultimately over the next few months I'm going to be out and about and talking to health workers, working with people in the system, understanding where the issues are, where improvements need to be made, where things are going well. "

Crucially, Ms Stephen-Smith has held onto the health infrastructure portfolio, which oversees the new hospital build.

"I really thought it was important to retain health infrastructure responsibilities at this time because we're in a critical point for the new Northside Hospital and I've been involved throughout this process," Ms Stephen-Smith said.

"We're coming towards the end of the very early contractor involvement stage, and this is a critical moment.

"It's about providing that continuity for some of our really important health infrastructure projects that are either in critical phases or coming to fruition, and then providing some support still in the health portfolio for the incoming minister to make sure that we can work together and I can support her as she transitions to the portfolio."

Outgoing ACT health minister Rachel Stephen-Smith says Canberra Health Services has significantly improved its emergency department performance. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

'A major problem'

But Opposition Leader Mark Parton is not confident the change in ministers will yield a different outcome for Canberra’s health system.

Mr Parton told ABC Radio Canberra the health portfolio was "clearly not" in good condition.

"There's all sorts of problems, ranging from waiting lists to culture, to problems with delivery of services," he said.

"It's a major, major problem.

"You can rearrange the deck chairs on the Titanic as much as you like, but I don't think it's going to make much difference."

title: Hunter transmission line approved after rerouting around homes, frogs
text:
A controversial transmission line project spanning the NSW Hunter region has received conditional approval from the New South Wales government after its route was amended to avoid landholders and endangered frogs.

The Hunter Transmission Project (HTP) will connect renewable power generated by two renewable energy zones (REZ) adjacent to the Hunter, the Central West Orana and New England REZs, to large population centres on the east coast.

The 500-kilovolt transmission line will span more than 100 kilometres from Bayswater in the Upper Hunter to Olney near Lake Macquarie and will include the construction of 200 large towers, with 90 per cent to be built on government or mining land.

NSW Premier Chris Minns said he understood the approval would be controversial, especially among impacted landholders.

"It will probably hit us politically but we don't have a choice," he said.

NSW Premier Chris Minns speaking in the Hunter region this week. (ABC News: Bridget Murphy)

"We have to make responsible decisions to deliver power for consumers and businesses, and if we don't make decisions like that then you'll see power prices go higher than they already currently are.

"We have to keep pressing ahead with energy needs for the state, and if we don't it will have big impacts on jobs and the economy."

Frog habitat impacts

Parts of the state-approved HTP route will run through parts of the Olney State Forest and the Watagans Ranges, which is one of three known homes of the endangered Littlejohn's tree frog.

EnergyCo executive project director Peter Redwin told ABC Newcastle Breakfast that the department had redesigned the route to "minimise impacts on their breeding areas".

Breeding habitats for the endangered Littlejohn's tree frog are within the Watagans area. (Supplied: University of Newcastle)

"We know of 62 breeding ponds that have been there and we are not going to impact 60 of those," he said.

"In addition to that we are actually helping the University of Newcastle with their breeding program for that tree frog. We've been told by our experts that we will not have a serious impact on that particular species."

He said that would involve relocation which the department "cannot avoid".

Aussie Ark, a Hunter-based conservation group has long campaigned against the project, fearing its approval will have a "catastrophic" impact on the endangered frog population.

Lead conservation officer Hayley Shute said today's decision was an "absolute nightmare" for the species.

"They're called a Littlejohn's tree frog … not a Littlejohn's pond frog," Ms Shute said.

"Yes, they can come down to the ponds to breed, but where are they going to come from … they actually live in the trees and that is what they're removing.

" Once those trees are gone and the shade's gone they're just open to predation. "

Ms Shute said the concerns raised by researchers and conservationists have fallen on "deaf ears".

"They've just gone ahead, ticked their boxes and they are basically ruining any chance of survival for this species in the Watagans," she said.

Land and housing

The ABC has previously spoken to landholders whose properties were subject to acquisition or negotiated purchasing from EnergyCo to build the HTP.

The human cost of energy security Hunter landowners in the path of transmission lines say they are living through the "most stressful experience" of their lives.

Initially the project was poised to impact around 70 private properties along the original route, but that has been reduced to "fewer than 20" with the amended route, according to a statement from NSW Energy Minister Penny Sharpe.

EnergyCo's Peter Redwin said there has been "positive" negotiation and collaboration with impacted owners.

"We've got a few last landowners that we're still dealing with, but our aim is that we will not go through compulsory acquisition, that we will do it through negotiation and we've been very successful on that to date," he said.

NSW Shadow Minister for Natural Resources and Upper Hunter Nationals MP Dave Layzell said it was commendable the majority of the infrastructure will avoid private property.

Upper Hunter Nationals MP Dave Layzell wants the construction process to benefit the region long-term. (Supplied: Dave Layzell MP)

"There's always areas of improvement that I would have liked to see, but overall I can say they have done their best to minimise the impacts so that it reduces the impact on landholders, maximises the amount of land that is government owned or mining land," he said.

The Minns government touted the construction of the HTP would create more than 800 jobs, primarily in the wider construction phase, with 160 to be based in the Hunter.

Mr Layzell said there was the potential that worker camps could be built for this project and other REZ projects which he would like to see benefit local communities long-term.

"One of my biggest criticisms of EnergyCo … is that in the time of a housing crisis these projects are talking about building large work camps," he said.

"These large work camps are going to be built, they take in up to 300 people, and at the end of the project they get completely demolished and removed.

"Why aren't we keeping some of this housing?"

The project will require a further rubber-stamp from the federal government before it can proceed.

EnergyCo said it will aim to begin construction in mid-2027.

title: Australia's biggest gold miner called to help stabilise WA's power issues
text:
Australia's biggest gold miner is being asked to carry a larger load to resolve decades of power capacity and reliability woes in WA's electricity network.

The owner of Kalgoorlie's Super Pit gold mine, Northern Star Resources, is negotiating commercial terms with government-owned utility Western Power to supply additional back-up power to the historic mining city.

Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said the plan would ensure there was no repeat of the 2024 blackouts which hit the city in the peak of summer, and would help limit outages that have plagued the city for decades.

A newly signed memorandum of understanding commits up to 70 megawatts of electricity supply from the 110-megawatt Parkeston power station at Kalgoorlie, which Northern Star jointly owns with Canadian electricity wholesaler TransAlta.

It shapes as a transformative deal for Kalgoorlie-Boulder, which sits on the eastern edge of the South West Interconnected System (SWIS), connected via a 655km-long transmission line in place since 1984.

The view down Boulder's historic Burt Street with the Super Pit gold mine in the background. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"We looked at a range of options and models, including government-owned and operated, and we went to market," Ms Sanderson said.

"Essentially we enter into an arrangement with Northern Star to use their Parkeston facility, and any excess power.

" It means should we have any catastrophic event on that main transmission line, we can get that backup running quickly so people don't experience long-term blackouts. "

The Parkeston power station is jointly owned by TransAlta and gold miner Northern Star Resources and has fed additional power into the grid during previous outages. (ABC Goldfields: Robert Koenig-Luck)

Power boost on horizon

The proposal also includes plans to expand capacity once Northern Star builds a new 140-megawatt thermal power station and a separate 366-megawatt renewable facility, which would include up to 32 wind turbines and 230,000 solar panels.

Northern Star's chief technical officer, Steve McClare, said both projects would deliver lower electricity inputs for the $1.6 billion expansion of the Super Pit's Fimiston Mill.

"They are in the very final stages, and we are going into that this financial year," he said.

The company has forecast expenditure of at least $160 million on the thermal power station, using natural gas and diesel generation.

Steve McClare and Kalgoorlie Consolidated Gold Mines general manager Nick Strong overseeing construction of the new Fimiston Mill in 2025. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Four outages a month

It is set to provide a significant boost to power security in the Goldfields, where WA's peak resources industry body has been calling for "urgent improvements".

The Chamber of Minerals and Energy said its Goldfields membership reported an average of four power outages a month during 2025.

It also estimated wholesale power costs for large industrial customers using the grid have doubled since 2020, rising from about $125 per megawatt-hour to as much as $250 last year.

The estimate formed part of a public submission to the Economic Regulation Authority, which has been reviewing Western Power's access arrangements to the grid.

The mining industry has been calling for "urgent improvements" to the Goldfields energy grid. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Among the newest industrial users to connect to the grid was Lynas Rare Earths, which commissioned its Kalgoorlie cracking and leaching plant in late 2024.

It reported losing the equivalent of one month's production due to power supply disruptions last November, and continues to be hampered by ongoing outages.

Similarly, Kalgoorlie gold miner Evolution Mining is assessing plans for a potential wind farm, after losing three days of production during the June quarter due to power outages.

Lynas Rare Earths opened its $800 million cracking and leaching plant at Kalgoorlie in November 2024. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Interim Lynas chief executive Pol Le Roux said the number of outages had reduced in recent months, but the company was still weighing up its own off-grid solution.

"It's true the power supply is not up to where we want it to be," he said.

"The situation has improved, there was some modifications made on the Western Power side.

"We are staying within one power failure per month, which is not what we wish to have, but it's what we have; I would say it's manageable."

Miners say grid reliability has improved in recent months. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Long-term plan for battery

It comes as the WA government considers applications by more than 20 potential bidders to fulfil Labor's election promise to build a $150 million vanadium flow battery in Kalgoorlie-Boulder.

Ms Sanderson said the emerging technology could create about 150 local jobs.

"They're evaluating all of those business cases that were received and out of that a preferred proponent will be selected, and that's done by an independent panel with a recommendation to government," she said.

Premier Roger Cook has previously said Kalgoorlie-Boulder's 50-megawatt battery would be operational by 2029, around the same time WA was scheduled to shut the last of its coal-fired power stations.

title: Judge slams law firm over delayed $120m payout to sacked Qantas workers
text:
A Federal Court judge has delivered a sharp rebuke to a class action law firm for delaying compensation to sacked Qantas workers, saying he has "no confidence" in the process and the firm would have to wear the consequences of breaching his court orders.

Maurice Blackburn Lawyers has been handling a $120 million payout that Qantas agreed to pay its illegally sacked workers in 2024, following a four-year Federal Court battle between the airline and the Transport Workers Union.

Workers were also expecting a share of $40 million, part of a penalty the court imposed on Qantas.

But the Federal Court heard Maurice Blackburn Lawyers only raised the alarm eight days ago that it needed more time to work out the complex payments.

Justice Michael Lee slapped down the law firm for coming to him at "a minute to midnight," and refused to deal with the request before the July 31 deadline, saying he was not given enough time to consider it properly.

It means 1,820 Qantas workers who the court found were illegally sacked in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic will have to wait longer to receive their compensation.

Workers were also expecting a share of $40 million, part of a penalty the court imposed on Qantas. (AAP: Paul Miller)

Law firm requests time extension

In its application for an extension of time, the law firm said it was struggling with the number of claimants, getting accurate medical reports and working with tax issues and Services Australia.

Maurice Blackburn Lawyers was meant to provide a schedule of payments made in the $120 million payout to the court by Friday, so the rest of the money could be apportioned to workers.

Justice Lee told the court Maurice Blackburn Lawyers must have known much earlier that it was going to miss his court-ordered deadline.

"I confess to being disturbed that almost six years after the outsourcing decision, the court is now being asked … to abandon a timetable which it had every reason to believe was realistic when it was fixed only seven months ago," he said.

He also reprimanded the firm's lawyers for writing to him personally asking for more time, instead of initially filing an application to have the matter dealt with in open court.

"Applications affecting the rights and expectations of more than 1,800 people ought to be brought openly," he said.

"Court orders are not like the traffic lights in Palermo.

"They are not there merely to be observed when it is thought convenient to do so."

Maurice Blackburn Lawyers put in an application for an extension of time. (ABC News: Michael Parfitt)

Barrister for Maurice Blackburn Lawyers, Adam Hochroth SC, told the court he wanted the matter dealt with on Wednesday, because his client's deadline was just two days away.

But Justice Lee said he would deal with the matter next week instead.

"Yes and you'll be in breach of [the deadline], and we'll see what consequences flow from that," he replied.

Qantas has been contacted for comment.

A spokesperson for Maurice Blackburn Lawyers said they would not comment on Wednesday's proceedings, but provided the ABC with a statement which said the law firm was experienced in class actions.

"The work is detailed and complex and requires the Administrator to engage on an individual basis with all claimants," the statement said.

"We anticipate that claimants will be advised of the estimated amount they will be eligible to receive shortly."

Workers not yet able to 'move on'

Don Dixon was sacked by Qantas. (ABC News: Isobel Roe)

Outside court, sacked worker Don Dixon said he wanted the case to be over, so he could "get his life back".

"A lot of people have financial situations that are terrible," he said.

"They really need that compensation for their health and to move on financially and pay the bills they haven't been able to pay."

Transport Workers Union national secretary Michael Kaine said Maurice Blackburn Lawyers won the case for workers, but "now it needs to step up to deliver the compensation these workers deserve into their pockets".

Justice Lee said the court was holding over $35 million that "should be in the hands of workers" and that it could not be distributed until the initial $120 million payout was finalised.

"Payment has become dependent upon a delayed administration outside the court's direct supervision, and which, on the present material, I have no confidence I know will be completed."

He said he would deal with the matter on August 6, when he had more time to consider it properly.

title: US school pauses humanoid robot plan after link with sexbot company raised
text:
A school district in a rural corner of upstate New York is hitting pause on plans to deploy an AI-powered, humanoid robot in the classroom after concerns about the maker's ties to a company that produces hyper-realistic sexbots.

The Salamanca City Central School District's board approved the nearly $US60,000 ($86,000) purchase from Realbotix, with visions that "Sally," as the stationary robot with long dark hair has already been nicknamed, would enhance the education of high school students studying robotics and technology fields.

Football and athletics among events as China launches 'Robot Olympics' The World Humanoid Robot Games kicks off in China as 280 teams from 16 countries compete in events such as football, track and field and table tennis.

But as news spread in the small community located on the Seneca Nation of Indians reservation, parents and teachers worried about how students' personal information would be used.

Unionised teachers aimed at Realbotix's sex doll sister company, Realdoll, even as district officials and the company itself stressed the two manufacturers operate independently.

"A robot built by a company associated with sex dolls has no business in our classrooms," Melinda Person, president of the union New York State United Teachers, said.

For now, the robot pilot remains on hold as the district works through "enhanced student data privacy agreements" with the state education officials and continues outreach to the community, according to a statement the district posted on its Facebook page.

Concerns about robot's role

New York State Education Commissioner Betty Rosa said she remained concerned about the robot's role in the classroom even after her staff met with district officials.

"Although you confirmed that the robot would not have any role delivering classroom instruction, a recent presentation to the board characterised the robot as a 'tutoring platform," Ms Rosa wrote in a letter to the district.

Chinese humanoid robot beats human half-marathon world record The winner from a Chinese smartphone maker reportedly completed the 21-kilometre race in 50 minutes and 26 seconds.

She also echoed residents' concerns about what data privacy and security protections would be in place.

Unionised teachers suggested the effort was a first step toward replacing flesh-and-bone educators.

"Sally" will be able to move its arms and hands but has non-working legs.

"Our students don't need robots," Ms Person said.

" They need real relationships with caring adults. "

District officials defend robot purchase

School superintendent Mark Beehler said the pilot, which also includes rollout of a virtual, AI-powered teacher's assistant and an at-home tutoring program, is not about replacing staff.

"There is no possible way a robot can replace a human in a school," he said.

"Even if it were possible, it would in no way be in the best interest of students.

"Teaching is a human-to-human process."

Mr Beehler, who was connected to Realbotix through a former colleague, said the Las Vegas-based company was a natural fit because its robots were already programmed with WozEd, a curriculum from Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak that the district uses.

Salamanca schools has posted "Sally" will not be collecting students' personal information. (X: Salamanca CCSD)

Last year, a San Diego charter school rolled out two AI-powered robots purchased from Engineered Arts, a robotics company based in the United Kingdom, for $US500,000.

Salamanca Schools, in social media posts, stressed that "Sally" would not be collecting students' personal information, recording audio or video of its interactions or sending data back to Realbotix.

The robot also has been programmed to steer clear of inappropriate topics such as sex, violence and gambling, and it will not be able to search the public internet or draw answers from unvetted generative AI services, according to the school district's social media post.

Instead, all information on "Sally" will be stored locally, with the life-sized robot consuming roughly the same amount of energy as a laptop, according to the district.

Robot maker responds to criticism

Realbotix said that student authentication would be handled through the district's existing systems, and any student-linked information would remain encrypted and under the district's control.

The company also pushed back at suggestions that "Sally" was simply a repurposed sex doll, saying it was a "newly manufactured, purpose-built educational unit" with no modified hardware.

Australia's AI revolution Australia this week made an important step forward in grappling with the AI revolution.

The school's robot comes from Realbotix LLC, which focuses on healthcare, education and other non-adult commercial applications.

A sister company, Intima LLC, holds an ownership stake in Realdoll, a longtime maker of sex dolls, including a line of AI-powered models billed as the "world's most advanced sex robot".

"Realbotix LLC and Intima LLC have different product offerings with no crossover," the company said in a statement.

"The two subsidiaries maintain their own management, personnel, payroll, facilities, manufacturing operations, product development, and market strategies."

Opportunity to access emerging technology

Mr Beehler argued that it was crucial for isolated districts like Salamanca, which is located along the Allegheny River near the Pennsylvania state line, to find new ways to introduce cutting-edge products into classrooms.

"In most cases, our students need to travel one to two hours to have opportunities to see emergent technology," he said.

Is 2025 ending with an AI bubble? What makes the AI-driven stock market bubble unique in history is that if it's not a bubble, the impact on humanity could be far more challenging than any previous technology.

"One of the intents of the robot is to help level the playing field and motivate students to continue studying robotics, AI, and STEAM-related career pathways."

Some Salamanca residents, though, remain unconvinced.

Joplin Ficek, who graduated from Salamanca High School in 2024 and now works at a daycare, said she did not see any reason to have robots or AI take such a prominent role at her old school at all.

"They just need to hire more people who are willing to put in the effort for the children," she said.

" They need more interaction with the children than having some robot raise our kids. "

title: Gold Coast nurse with rare disorder awaiting third kidney transplant
text:
Gold Coast nurse Daniel Hoepner spends his days responding to medical emergencies and helping save lives.

But, unbeknown to many of the patients he cares for, he is also waiting for life-saving treatment of his own.

The 30-year-old is living with kidney failure and is waiting for his third kidney transplant after being diagnosed with a rare disease shortly after birth.

Despite spending six hours every second day on haemodialysis to filter his blood, Mr Hoepner continues to work full-time as a clinical nurse consultant in the Clinical Response Unit across Gold Coast University Hospital and Robina Hospital.

Daniel Hoepner was diagnosed with congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type. (Supplied: Daniel Hoepner)

"I definitely don't make it known to patients. I think they've got enough going on to not be worrying about their nurse being unwell," he said.

"But I actually found when I wasn't working, I was a lot more tired.

" [Work is] something to take my mind off it, something to do, keep my brain active, and obviously my body active too. "

Mr Hoepner has spent his entire life in and out of hospital after being born with congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type (CNF), a severe genetic disorder that causes the kidneys to leak large amounts of protein into the urine.

The condition leads to severe swelling, kidney failure and, ultimately, requires dialysis and kidney transplantation for survival.

"When I was born, my mum saw something was wrong. I was just like a little football, really swollen," he said.

"She took me to a couple of doctors and they kind of just said I was just a fat baby, which is normally a good thing but, in this case, it wasn't, unfortunately."

Daniel Hoepner continues to work as a nurse. (Supplied: Gold Coast Health)

Because he was too small for a transplant, Mr Hoepner began dialysis as a baby and remained on treatment until he was six years old, when he received his first kidney transplant from his stepfather.

The transplant gave him more than 16 years of improved health before it began to fail, just as he was starting his nursing career.

"I'd just finished university and had just started a job," he said.

"Then I just started becoming a lot more unwell."

His mother wanted to donate one of her kidneys but was not a suitable match.

Instead, she donated to a stranger through the Australia and New Zealand paired kidney exchange program, which in turn allowed Mr Hoepner to receive a compatible kidney from another donor.

But now, that second transplant is failing and Mr Hoepner has once again joined the donor list.

This time, it's his partner who has stepped forward, offering to donate her kidney in the hope it will lead to Mr Hoepner receiving another life-saving transplant.

Daniel Hoepner with his family. (Supplied: Daniel Hoepner)

While balancing full-time nursing with regular dialysis treatments is challenging, Mr Hoepner has learned to adapt.

"I've always wanted to work in a profession where I could make a real difference in people's lives during some of their most difficult moments," he said.

"Even now, after becoming a dialysis patient myself, that motivation hasn't changed.

"I've learned to be organised, listen to my body and make the most of the time I have.

" Nursing is a huge part of who I am, and continuing to work gives me a sense of purpose and normality beyond being a patient. "

The latest figures from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare show just over 1,000 kidney transplants were performed across Australia in 2024.

Natasha Rogers, the head of transplantation at Westmead Hospital, said while transplant numbers continued to rise, receiving three or more kidney transplants remained uncommon.

"We have the Australia and New Zealand Dialysis and Transplant Registry that reports on all the kidney-transplant activity across the nation and probably only about 1 to 2 per cent of recipients will have had three or more kidney transplants," Professor Rogers said.

"So, it's pretty unusual."

Natasha Rogers says receiving three or more kidney transplants is uncommon. (Supplied)

Regardless, she said Mr Hoepner's ability to continue working while undergoing dialysis was "impressive".

"Having kidney disease and having to do dialysis is a full-time job by itself. It's very labour-intensive," she said.

" Dialysis does not make you feel great and you go from one treatment to the next to stay alive, essentially, and to pair that with full-time work is amazing. "

Although Mr Hoepner doesn't know when a suitable kidney will become available, he hopes sharing his experience will encourage others facing similar challenges not to put their lives on hold.

"Keep making memories, keep setting goals, and keep hoping," he said.

"A transplant can give you a new chapter, but your life is still worth living today."

title: Taylor denies giving money to group at centre of NSW corruption probe
text:
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has denied he ever gave money to a Liberal faction at the centre of a NSW corruption probe into branch stacking.

The right-wing group known as the NSW Reformers included former Liberal staffer Dylan Whitelaw, who had a loose association with Mr Taylor through Catholic Schools NSW boss Dallas McInerney.

During a hearing on Tuesday before the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), Mr Whitelaw was shown a screenshot of a message sent from lobbyist Robert Assaf to a group chat including key figures being investigated by the inquiry.

The screenshot was of a message exchange between Mr McInerney and Mr Assaf.

It read: "I have breakfast club with ministers this Thursday morning. Who can I get an update from? Re SCD progress in last six to 12 months. "I want to shake down Angus for 10k."

Mr Whitelaw said while he could not recall seeing the message, he assumed it was referring to federal Liberal MP and now opposition leader Mr Taylor.

Under repeated questioning on Wednesday, Mr Taylor denied five times he had made any payment.

"No payment was made," he said.

Asked if he disputed the text messages seen by the inquiry, he said he was "not a party to proceedings" and would not be giving a "running commentary".

"I'll let the commission do its job," he said.

Mr Taylor said he has not been approached by the commission and would not entertain "hypotheticals" about giving evidence.

Taylor will not say if he was asked to contribute

Pressed on whether he was ever asked to give money to the NSW Reformers group, Mr Taylor repeated his denial that a payment was made and would not confirm if he was aware of the group or its activities.

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the corruption watchdog that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday. These are some of the key players embroiled in the donations investigation.

The inquiry was shown another group chat message sent by Mr Whitelaw claiming Mr McInerney had secured a $15,000 payment and ongoing monthly donations of $3,000 for the group's work from Mr Taylor.

Mr Whitelaw said he did not remember sending the message or the donation being made.

"Potentially, Dallas [McInerney] had told me something that was incorrect," Mr Whitelaw said.

"I'd be very surprised if Mr Taylor made any financial contribution."

title: Son of a gun Hewitt takes top-100 scalp in ATP first
text:
Cruz Hewitt's victory in his ATP Tour main-draw debut is set to rocket the son of a gun up the world rankings.

Fresh off a run to the Wimbledon boys final, Hewitt beat former world number 37 Marcus Giron — currently ranked 85 — 6-3, 6-4 in Washington DC on Tuesday (Wednesday AEST).

The Australian, who didn't face a break point, became the fourth man born in 2008 or later to win a tour-level match and the youngest Washington match-winner since Japan's Kei Nishikori in 2007.

The teen qualified thanks to walkovers after leading both Dusan Lajovic and top-seed Zach Svajda and has surged 255 places to number 357 in the ATP's live rankings.

He'll play the winner of countryman and mentor Alex de Minaur and former world number three Stefanos Tsitsipas in the next round.

Cruz Hewitt's (right) win at the DC Open means he could face countryman Alex de Minaur next up in the round of 16. (Getty Images: Paul Morigi)

He had warmed up with father Lleyton, the former world number one, two-time major winner and 2004 Washington champion, who told him to lap up the moment.

"[He told me] mainly to enjoy it, because it was my first tour-level match … and to take every point one-by-one, to enjoy the atmosphere and to enjoy the crowd and that is what I did," he said.

Cruz said he was handling the pressure of carrying the Hewitt name "as best as I can".

"There is obviously a little bit of pressure, but I try to take the positives out of it as well, and I am happy with how I am dealing with it so far," he added.

"I am really happy with how I competed today. I came out and started pretty well, and I am thrilled to get through to the next round."

De Minaur is defending his title in the American capital and fresh off a two-day Portofino honeymoon after marrying fellow pro Katie Boulter in Tuscany last month.

"It was an amazing time, everything we could have ever imagined," said De Minaur, who is coming off the disappointment of an upset fourth-round Wimbledon loss.

"It was like our own little movie. We were able to celebrate with family and friends and have a very small honeymoon.

"Then we're on a flight here to Washington and getting our heads screwed back on and back to being tennis players."

title: Tradies swap swags for dongas on wheels to retain workers out bush
text:
Dolly Thompson is a woman of few words, but what she does say makes you listen.

She is an outback road worker who often spends weeks and even months living and working in some of the most remote corners of Queensland.

"I'm used to that kind of life, it doesn't worry me," Ms Thompson said.

"You're better off being out in the camp than what you are in town."

The roadside workers can be deployed anywhere in a large remote shire about the size of Tasmania. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

She may have a point. With a population of about 360, the Barcoo Shire Council's mobile road train accommodation is a far cry from the rough-and-ready camps of the past.

There is hope the mounted accommodation will attract more skilled workers to the bush and beat the competitive conditions of industries such as mining.

From swags to dongas on wheels

The triple-trailer road train is currently set up on the Quilpie to Windorah Road, while the Barcoo Shire has another mobile camp home at Windorah and another further west towards Birdsville.

The person in charge of this road camp is Jason Beilby, construction supervisor with the Barcoo Shire Council.

Jason Beilby has been working in outback Queensland for decades. (ABC Western Qld: Jay Carstens)

He has been working on Queensland's roads for about 20 years so he has seen and lived in very different accommodation.

"Ten years ago we were very rough camps," Mr Beilby said.

" We were living in the bush … and we found that to employ people we just had to upgrade, and that's fair enough. "

Today's road train accommodation is fitted with bedrooms and ensuites, kitchens, dining areas, laundries, and access to streaming services through personal and shared TVs.

A kitchen within a mobile road train camp has all the sauces you need. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

"They've got every little mod con that you can find," Mr Beilby said.

He said the workers enjoyed the more modern dongas which had helped attract more people to the job and retained them longer.

"We've got to employ people so we've got to give them good, comfortable accommodation," he said.

"Twelve hours out in the sun [and] you do want to come home to comfort, and that's a good sales point for employees to get them to come here and work."

A mobile roadside camp set-up using triple-trailer road trains between Windorah and Quilpie. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

Mr Beilby said another welcome feature was that the accommodation could be packed up quickly and moved to the next location.

"We back the trucks underneath, they're all on cables. They just lift all the verandahs up, and we move. It's very simple," he said.

"[In] some places we're 300 to 400 kilometres from the nearest town so they're pretty self-sufficient.

"I think all shires should upgrade, but it depends on their structure. [Our shire] is the size of Tasmania."

Roadside workers can stay on-site without having to drive hundreds of kilometres to accommodation. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

Community-driven ideas the engine-room

Keeping a secure workforce in remote towns can be particularly challenging compared to cities, or even rural communities, due to the distances involved.

Foundation for Rural and Regional Renewal's (FRRR) head of grants Jill Karena said that meant remote communities were often solving complex problems.

"Remote communities are not short of imagination and innovation," Ms Karena said.

"The distances are greater, the costs are higher, skilled workers can be much harder to access and keep, and the services often travel in-and-out."

Ms Karena said the best ideas often came from those who lived locally, but added that outside support through funding could help "back that ingenuity".

A spokesperson for the Barcoo Shire Council said the mobile workers' accommodation had improved its staff retention, having built triple-trailer road train accommodation camps since 2022.

All roadside workers in the main camp have remained with the council for more than five years, while some, like Ms Thompson, have stuck around for more than a decade.

There's plenty of skilled worker jobs in the west, but sometimes the mines get first dibs. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

"When I first come out I came out with my husband and learnt how to drive machinery and that," Ms Thompson said.

She stayed, in part because of the community and work culture.

"They're fun to be with. They all help out," she said.

title: FIFA boss unveils $US20b plan to sell World Cup to Kushner consortium
text:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino's plan to create a $US20 billion ($29 billion) company running the World Cup with private investors, including the Kushner family, has been attacked by European football body UEFA.

"It is not FIFA's to sell," UEFA said in a statement. "None of us are the owners of football."

Mr Infantino's plans to form a commercial subsidiary, called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run competitions like the World Cup and Club World Cup, were first reported by The Times of London.

Players and fans made the World Cup a success, but the politics shouldn't be forgotten The biggest ever World Cup brought diverse communities together and galvanised its non-traditional footballing co-hosts, but the concerns raised from the start have not disappeared in the positive afterglow.

FIFA said in a statement FFE would raise up to $US4.2 billion later this year to help fund development programs "based on an initial equity valuation of $US20 billion by carefully selecting long-term investors who will purchase minority, non-controlling interests".

FIFA is working with JP Morgan while intended investors include Thrive Eternal, launched by Joshua Kushner, whose brother Jared Kushner is a son-in-law of US President Donald Trump.

The men's World Cup that finished this month only deepened the political and personal ties between Mr Trump and Mr Infantino, and fuelled concerns about those ties, including from UEFA.

"The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially," UEFA said, responding to the reports of selling stakes in FIFA competitions.

FIFA is a Swiss-based not-for-profit association of its 211 national member federations worldwide.

The brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner (pictured), is among the potential World Cup investors. (Reuters: Kent Nishimura)

Those members must approve any plan and would get the chance "to access up to $US20 million in one-off capital", FIFA said.

"This is about the democratisation of football worldwide," Mr Infantino said in a FIFA statement, which added that "a consultation process has begun".

UEFA, however, said it took reports of the project "extremely seriously. So should every national Football Association".

"This crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross," said UEFA, which comprises 55 of the FIFA members.

FIFA emphasising financial benefits for members

FIFA boss Gianni Infantino has promised to "unleash the commercial potential" of the World Cup. (Getty Images)

FIFA said Mr Infantino had detailed the outline of Tuesday's surprise announcement to members who met in Manhattan on July 18 ahead of the World Cup final.

There, Mr Infantino promised to "unleash the commercial potential and opportunity that FIFA has".

FIFA's statement emphasised how much money each of its 211 members could get in the "FIFA Fast-Forward Program", running until 2038.

Instead of the promised $US8 million each in development funds in the 2027-30 World Cup commercial cycle, it would be $US20 million, then $US22 million and $US24 million in the following cycles.

FIFA banked record World Cup income of about $US12 billion from the 2026 tournament, which had unprecedentedly high prices for tickets and hospitality across the US, Canada and Mexico.

World Cup winners Spain will be one of six nations hosting matches at the 2030 World Cup.

It was unclear how that money could be matched from Spain, Portugal and Morocco co-hosting the 2030 men's edition.

Member federations could choose if they wanted to take part in the new financial opportunities, FIFA said.

"FIFA would retain sole control of FFE and exclusive authority over football governance, competitions, match calendar, and all regulatory and sporting decisions," the soccer body said.

FIFA's integrity standards were called into question during the World Cup, including by team coaches, Norway's soccer federation and a top European public body, the Council of Europe.

FIFA's previous attempt to privatise assets

Infantino has built stronger ties with Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman throughout his tenure as FIFA boss. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

Mr Infantino's 11-year FIFA presidency has become increasingly controversial, and this is the second time he has tried to push through a multi-billion-dollar deal with private backers.

In 2018 he proposed a secretive $US25 billion offer over 12 years with SoftBank of Japan to create new global competitions, including an expanded men's Club World Cup, seemingly backed by Saudi Arabian money.

That ultimately failed after meeting fierce resistance from UEFA, which saw threats to its prize assets: the Champions League and the European Championship.

Mr Infantino still built closer ties to Saudi soccer and the kingdom's Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman. Saudi Arabia will host the 2034 World Cup, and largely funded the revamped men's Club World Cup hosted in the US last year.

What does this mean for Infantino's future?

The financial success of the just-ended World Cup has made it likely that Mr Infantino will be re-elected unopposed next year for a fourth and final term in office through to 2031.

At his re-election in 2023 in Rwanda, Mr Infantino suggested any CEO delivering similar financial results would be kept in the job forever.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Speculation has swirled for years that Mr Infantino might want a different global role in soccer beyond his FIFA presidency, which is due to end when he is 61.

The Times reported on Tuesday that a CEO-like commissioner role of the new FFE operation could be created for him.

"This has never been discussed," FIFA said in a statement on Wednesday (AEST). "However, the FIFA president and the FIFA administration will and must have leading roles in this entity — if approved."

There was no timetable suggested for debate and decisions by FIFA, its ruling Council chaired by Mr Infantino, and the 211 members.

FIFA is scheduled to hold an online congress on November 23 to confirm hosts of the Women's World Cup editions in 2031 and 2035.

title: Quick hits: Record beaten five times in 10 minutes, pool haka thrills
text:
New Zealand swimmers pay tribute to a victorious teammate by performing the haka, a Pakistani lawn bowler fits in some work shifts and a weightlifting record falls a staggering five times.

Here are the quick hits from day five of the Commonwealth Games.

1. 'Super proud' New Zealanders

Lewis Clareburt and his New Zealand teammates perform the haka after his victory. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

New Zealand swimmer Lewis Clareburt received a double honour after winning the men's 400-metre individual medley final.

Aside from being awarded the gold medal, Clareburt was the recipient of a haka proudly performed by his New Zealand teammates.

The Tollcross International Swimming Centre crowd also appreciated the gesture.

"People really respect it [the haka] around the world and it makes me super proud to be a Kiwi," Clareburt told reporters.

The crowd erupted when the New Zealanders performed the haka. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Clareburt won the men's 200m butterfly earlier in the swimming program.

2. Lawn bowler works double shift

Mohammed Ayub Qureshi competing in the lawn bowls. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

No-one can accuse lawn bowler Mohammed Ayub Qureshi of not being a multitasker.

Qureshi competed for Pakistan in the men's singles event while also working at his restaurant in Glasgow.

Last Friday afternoon local time, he faced off against Scotland's Jason Banks before heading to the restaurant to work the evening rush.

Showing what the Commonwealth Games are all about, Qureshi invited Banks to drop by for a meal after the Scot sealed victory.

Loading Instagram content

"I was too scared before I played him in case he spiced up my food too much," Banks said.

It is the second time Qureshi has represented Pakistan at the Commonwealth Games in the city that has been his home for more than 50 years.

3. Record falls again and again

Hafizuddin Bin Roslin Muhammad ended a run of record-breaking lifts. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

What could possibly be better than seeing the Commonwealth record broken at a Commonwealth Games?

Well, seeing the same one be beaten five times in the space of 10 minutes or so would probably do it.

That is exactly what happened in the men's 88-kilogram weightlifting competition, with Cameron McTaggart, Braydon Kennedy and Hafizuddin Bin Roslin Muhammad all achieving new standards in rapid succession.

New Zealander McTaggart started things off with a 154kg lift.

That was swiftly bettered by Canada's Kennedy, who lifted 155kg with his first attempt.

McTaggart tried to better that, but missed at 157kg with his final snatch.

Then Malaysian lifter Muhammad entered the chat.

Neither he nor Kennedy could get 160kg up on their first attempts at the weight, but Muhammad did so on his second.

Then Kennedy threw up 161kg, so Muhammad added another kilo for the newest and final record of 162kg.

4. Aussies snare two golds in an hour

Breanna Scott won gold on the beam. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

Breanna Scott already had a gold medal from this Commonwealth Games when she stepped out onto the balance beam on Tuesday.

After she flipped off it at the end of her routine, she had a second.

"It's pretty overwhelming to be honest, none of it has sunk in yet," she told Channel Seven after the final.

"The team gold was such a special medal for all of us, and that was really the main goal coming into this.

"All of us in finals now getting these extra little medals is just topping it off."

She, and the rest of the Australian team, barely had time to let it, to be fair.

Jesse Moore delivered a superb routine to secure gold. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

An hour or so later, Australia had a second gold of the session.

Jesse Moore broke his duck to claim a sensational gold on the parallel bars.

His was Australia's ninth gymnastics medal of these Games.

5. Athlete on track twice in 34 minutes

Howard Tapuaiga Siila competing in the men's 800m heats. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

Howard Tapuaiga Siila knew he had a full schedule on his hands when he arrived at the Scotstoun Stadium on day five.

The Tuvalu athlete was entered in both the men's 400m and 800m heats, which is a daunting task at the best of times.

But for Siila, there was only 34 minutes between the start of each race.

He took off in his 800m heat at 11:33am local time, finishing eighth in 2:32.38.

Siila was back on the track for the 400m at 12:07pm, finishing eighth via a time of 55.96.

Both were season-best times.

Competing in both events was planned, but there was one hitch.

"When I decided to enter the races we weren't sure of the scheduling," Siila told reporters in the mixed zone.

title: Queensland nightlife tsar recommends liquor law overhaul
text:
The Queensland government has already ruled out a recommendation made by its night-life tsar to change holiday trading hours for licensed venues.

The Moonside report by the state's first nightlife commissioner, John "JC" Collins, was released today.

The former Powderfinger bassist has been tasked with reinvigorating the sector ahead of the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

Brisbane's nightlife commissioner John Collins, a former member of Powderfinger. (ABC News: Liz Pickering)

He has recommended the state review its liquor laws — including restrictions on Christmas and Easter and late-night trading — and how it handles noise complaints.

Collins said the state was "behind" in its regulations and put too much of a burden on venues.

"For too long the narrative has been the nightlife is a nuisance, and been treated that way," he said.

The report, handed to government late last year, recommends updating Queensland's decades-old liquor act, which restricts alcohol sales on Good Friday and Christmas Day and limits venues to six extended trading hours a year.

Youth Minister Sam O'Connor said changes to Christmas and Easter trading were off the table.

"We need to drive every day of the year, not just one particular day of trade," he said.

"It's usually the only day for those businesses where their hospitality workers will know that everyone won't be working at the same time, so you can have those staff get-togethers."

Queensland is preparing to up its nightlife ahead of the Brisbane 2032 Games. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

The review also recommends the government revises "outdated" sound regulations, which "unfairly penalise venues", and change the way sound is measured to "better balance community expectations with venue operations".

If adopted, five separate households would have to complain before compliance action was taken. Currently, a single noise complaint can trigger intervention.

Liquor license discount

The government has committed to the recommendation to make liquor licenses cheaper for live music venues.

Licenses can cost tens of thousands of dollars a year, but there is no figure on that discount yet.

"It will be a discount that will make a difference," Mr O'Connor said.

"And every dollar in the pocket of these venues, particularly these small venues, is more money that they can invest into having live music."

The review also recommends the government revises "outdated" sound regulations, which "unfairly penalise venues". (Unsplash: Pim Myten)

Big touring acts will also get a booking fee discount at state-owned venues if they include local acts in their line-up.

'We have to be open after 8:30'

The report also looks at how to encourage more eateries to open later.

This is not limited by regulations, but by people's behaviour, Collins said.

"Queenslanders are first up and first to bed, and that's ok, but we've got to try to make the framework that gets people having dining experiences after 8 o'clock," he said.

"If we're going to invite the world here, we have to be open after 8:30."

NationalWACity life ‘Perhaps consider Northbridge’: Perth CBD adult store’s sex-on-premises plans knocked back Indigo Lemay-Conway July 29, 2026 — 1:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

City of Perth councillors have gone against staff recommendations and denied an adult store’s request to operate a sex-on-premises site in the heart of the city, suggesting they take it to Northbridge instead. While three elected members voted in support of the Pink Rabbit Club venue on Barrack Street operating as an LGBTQI+ community safe space, the vote on Tuesday night required an absolute majority and thus failed to get over the line. The building located at 129 Barrack Street, currently operates as an adult retail shop – known as Pink Rabbit Adult Boutique. Michael Philipps The development application sought to allow the Pink Rabbit Club to run an adults-only exclusive club for consensual sexual activities at 129 Barrack Street. Currently, the building operates as an adult retail shop – known as Pink Rabbit Adult Boutique – on the ground floor, but the development application would see the upper floor become a space for “social connection, education and consensual sexual activity”.

Advertisement

The report to council noted the applicant, Rowe Group, described the space as being designed to “foster a sex-positive, inclusive, and affirming environment for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, and other identities within the community”. “As an 18+ exclusive club, it emphasises social connection, education, and consensual intimate activities in a non-judgmental setting. Members are united by a shared interest in fostering LGBTQI+ community connections, including safe discussions, social interactions, and consensual activities (including those of sexual nature) that support personal expression and well-being,” the applicant said in the report. Speaking in favour of the venue, councillor Liam Gobbert said the proposal offered no reasons for objection. “Should the clientele be a factor in determining this matter, it would amount to an interference, I believe, in a landowner’s private enjoyment of their lot,” he said. “I do think it is worth mentioning, though, having said that, that the proposed clientele to being the LGBTQIA+ community is a good thing.

Advertisement

“Safe spaces for any historically or contemporaneously marginalised, disadvantaged, or persecuted parts of the community are a good thing, and that a private landowner is seeking to provide that type of a safe space in our city without government support should be seen as a good thing.” Related Article City life Perth CBD ‘sex-on-premise’ venue tipped for approval despite community backlash Councillor Lisa Ma, who also supported the proposal, said the council should respond directly to the concerns raised by the community about this item “because, underneath the language of location and antisocial behaviour, the real discomfort for many is the sex-on-premises nature of this venue”. “So on location, let’s be honest about what’s really being asked: not ‘is Barrack Street suitable’, but ‘should this kind of activity exist anywhere in our city at all?’,” she said. “Sex-on-premises venues aren’t exactly new or exotic. They operate lawfully across Australian capital cities, always as private membership-based clubs, and precisely because of that, that structure keeps the activity consensual, controlled, and out of the public view.

Advertisement

“Again, this proposal follows that exact model: upstairs, no signage, no street presence, members only. If we reject here on locational grounds, in my opinion, we’re not solving a planning problem. “We’re saying we’d rather this activity stay unregulated and out of sight somewhere we don’t have to think about.” Despite their championing for the approval, fellow council members were not prepared to budge. Councillor Catherine Lezer said there was a place for inclusive safe spaces in the city – but it was not on Barrack Street. “The submissions and the ratepayers tell me a venue for adult activity does not belong here,” she said.

Advertisement

“Barrack Street in 2026 is a vastly different place from the COVID-recovery vacancy landscape of 2022, when the Pink Rabbit retail-only store was approved. There are now shops, cafés, restaurants, family apartments, hotels, renovated heritage buildings, and Barrack Street continues to improve. “I urge the owner to perhaps consider Northbridge, an entertainment precinct suited for this type of venue. This is simply the wrong use in the wrong place.” Similarly, councillor Chris Patten said an entertainment precinct would be a “much better location” for a sex-on-premises site. Councillor Viktor Ko said one of his main concerns was that members would have to pay for a membership to attend the venue. “I cannot agree with charging for membership. It goes against the model of inclusion. It goes against the model of actually including and welcoming people,” he said.

Advertisement

“And from my research, I can’t find any other business in the city that actually offers the same service as this. So if we do approve this, this will be one of its one of its only businesses in the city that offers this.” Related Article Planning and development ‘Like a fishbowl’: Perth heritage precinct, mosque unite against eight-storey tower Gobbert warned that refusal of the development application could result in an expensive State Administrative Tribunal hearing. “I couldn’t see any [reasons] in this DA. Is there a legitimate reason to refuse the DA, and what’s the going rate for defending a SAT case at the moment? Is it $25,000 to $30,000 of ratepayers money?” he asked the council staff. Acting chief executive Maria Cooke said amenity impact claims were not strong enough to warrant a refusal, and that SAT rates, depending on the length of the hearing, could cost tens of thousands of dollars.

The recommendation to approve the sex-on-premises site was lost 4-3. Councillors Raj Doshi and Adam Pacan were absent from the meeting and therefore did not vote. Perth Lord Mayor Bruce Reynolds made an alternative motion to refuse the application because the venue would “adversely impact upon the amenity and character of the locality … by way of adverse noise, reduced public safety, and residential and social behaviour”. It was approved 5-2 with councillors Ma and Gobbert voting against it.

title: Patriot expands footprint in heart of Zambian copper country
text:

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Patriot expands footprint in heart of Zambian copper country Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward July 29, 2026 — 12:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Patriot Resources has bolted on another slice of highly prospective ground in the heart Zambia’s world class copper belt, acquiring a 90 per cent interest in a strategic licence. The tenement sits just 17 kilometres along strike from First Quantum Minerals’ soon-to-be producing Fishtie project which is expected to ramp up to a production rate of about 30,000 tonnes of copper a year by the end of the decade. The company paid just US$50,000 (A$71,600) for its majority stake in the 16.15-square-kilometre licence, with US$20,000 (A$28,700) paid on signing and the balance due on completion. The vendor will be free-carried on the remaining 10 per cent interest. Patriot Resources has acquired a new licence in the Zambian Copperbelt, hosted in similar stratigraphy as Ivanhoe Mines giant Kamoa copper mine in the DRC. The new ground, located 12km north of Mkushi, is believed to cover the south-western extension of the Lusale Basin mineralised corridor – a significant geological feature which forms part of a neighbourhood that has hosted some of the largest copper deposits in the world. The basin is considered a satellite of the revered Central African copper belt that straddles the border between Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). For a junior explorer, securing ground with a geological address close to some of the world’s premier copper deposits represents a serious coup for this sub-$20m market cap company.

Advertisement

Patriot says the mineralisation style is hosted in a stratigraphic position that shares many similarities to what churned out Ivanhoe Mines’ colossal, 34 million tonnes of contained copper, Kamoa deposit in the DRC and the Lonshi deposit on the eastern flank of the Zambian Copperbelt. Patriot’s new tenement sits within the Katanga Supergroup, an approximately 7km-thick sequence of rocks that hosts the majority of the region’s prolific copper and cobalt deposits. The acquisition complements the company’s recent success at its Tonic prospect, within the Mumbwa project area also in Zambia. Maiden reverse circulation drilling at Tonic in early July confirmed notable copper-silver-zinc-cobalt mineralisation from surface. One hole delivered a solid 17 metre hit at 0.41 per cent copper, 4.7 grams per tonne (g/t) silver and 0.30 per cent zinc from 29m. That interval included a higher-grade core of 7 metres grading 0.78 per cent copper, 5.1g/t silver and 0.38 per cent zinc from 30m. Patriot says the Tonic system remains open at depth and along strike, with most of its defined induced polarisation, or “IP” footprint yet to feel the drill bit. The target corridor now steps out to the southeast from Tonic for a total distance of 5.5km. Importantly, the targets line up along the same northwest-southeast trending Mumbwa Fault Zone that hosts Sinomine Resource Group’s, 675,000 tonnes of contained copper, Kitumba deposit, a mere 18km from Tonic.

Advertisement

Notably, the nearby infrastructure angle adds further appeal to the address with The Kitumba development including a processing facility and copper smelter due for commissioning this year. Whilst copper in Zambia is clearly a major focus, Patriot is also advancing its impressive Tassa silver-gold play in Peru, where a recent re-assay program has successfully validated historical grades ahead of a planned maiden drill campaign. The validation is a critical step, as Tassa already features a JORC-compliant inferred resource of 31.4 million silver-equivalent ounces grading a solid 52.68 grams per tonne silver equivalent. The real blue sky was unveiled in May when Patriot blew out the project’s conceptual exploration target to a mammoth range of between 559 million and 774 million silver-equivalent ounces. The addition of a Zambian copper play looks to have completed a trifecta of near-term activity priorities for Patriot. A phase-two drill campaign at its Tonic copper discovery, geophysics and mapping at its newly acquired licence in Zambia, and a maiden drill program to test the scale of its Tassa silver project in Peru now all loom large. Additionally, Patriot continues its divestment strategy for its Gorman lithium project in Ontario, Canada, signalling a clear focus on its most promising assets in tier-one jurisdictions.

The company looks to have been to be picking up assets based on postcodes carefully. By securing ground with geological similarities to a world-beating deposit and located just down the road from a major player, Patriot has given itself a good chance of clocking a discovery. With drill rods set to turn in the coming months at Tassa and Tonic, and plenty of news flow to come, this ASX-junior is worth keeping an eye on. title: MCG double header highlights blockbuster finale to AFL season
text:
The 2026 AFL home-and-away season will finish with a bang, the final two rounds of the campaign even featuring two games at the MCG in the one day.

The league released details of the 18 games across rounds 23 and 24 on Wednesday.

Traffic in the Sicilian capital of Palermo is notoriously chaotic. Lights there, at least in the popular imagination, are regarded as offering mere guidelines to motorists. “Court orders are not like the traffic lights in Palermo,” Justice Michael Lee said to a Sydney courtroom. “They are not there merely to be observed when it is thought convenient to do so.” Justice Michael Lee, who put Qantas to the rhetorical sword in an earlier judgment, rounded on lawyers representing its sacked workers. The firm would be in breach of court orders, Lee said, and he signalled potential punishments. Lee questioned why the delays “only became apparent in mid-June, despite issues developing over months”, and why he had not been informed earlier. “What ought not occur is that the court is presented, at one minute to midnight, with what was presented as a fait accompli,” Lee said.

He rejected the request by Maurice Blackburn to alter orders made last year that compensation for fired Qantas ground staff be completed by July 31, 2026 and scheduled a longer hearing on the matter for August 6. “You’ll be in breach of [the orders by then], and we’ll see what consequences flow from that,” Lee said, though he cautioned that the firm may have a good explanation for the delay. He suggested the court may need to change the process for at least part of the amount that workers are owed because he had “no confidence” that Maurice Blackburn’s process would be completed in a timely fashion. But only $5 million of the money has been paid so far, as Maurice Blackburn tries to calculate the financial and intangible loss suffered by each worker. The Transport Workers’ Union expressed hope that workers would soon be paid. The union had brought the case against Qantas in 2020 after the airline sacked the workers in part to stop them from exercising a legal right to take industrial action as they bargained for more pay. “These workers, backed by their union, won this case against all odds when not even the Coalition government was standing up to Qantas’ decision,” said TWU national secretary Michael Kaine. “Maurice Blackburn added its experience, having fought and won other significant worker cases. But now it needs to step up to deliver the compensation these workers deserve into their pockets,” Kaine said. Maurice Blackburn had no comment on the Wednesday hearing. text:
