Key points THEATRE: Melbourne Theatre Company’s Uncle Vanya offers up sardonic one-liners

MUSIC: Silversun Pickups at the Forum is all about losing yourself in the sound

MUSIC: ACO’s From Winter’s Stillness is an edgy musical hybrid

THEATRE

Uncle Vanya ★★★★

Melbourne Theatre Company, Arts Centre Melbourne, until August 22 It’s a rare and charming thing to see Uncle Vanya done in period dress, as it is in Anne-Louise Sarks’ latest production for the MTC, on a splendid set that evokes a crumbling provincial estate in the last decade of the 19th century. Singling out actors for praise in Chekhov may be inevitable but always feels like a betrayal. Pia Johnson Contemporary Chekhovian performance tends to modernise, reframe, relocate. It’s as if we wanted to fire a bullet at the past – an exercise in futility, as Vanya himself discovers twice. Time doesn’t work that way. Playwright Joanna Murray-Smith believes (rightly) that such modernising is unnecessary in a good Chekhov production. Her Vanya adaptation gives a light textual massage for clarity, to draw out the comedy and update the vernacular.

Advertisement

As you’d expect from Murray-Smith, the sardonic one-liners are mercilessly sharp, and characters slip in words like “f---wit” and “bonking”, while being aware enough to admit that, well, “No one says ‘bonking’ any more.” Beyond that and the sound design – the Violent Femmes’ Add It Up doesn’t feel appropriate to the general vibe – it’s a faithful, lightly periodised production and an excellent intro to Chekhovian tragicomedy. It’s a rare and charming thing to see Uncle Vanya done in period dress. Pia Johnson Singling out actors for praise in Chekhov may be inevitable but always feels like a betrayal. Star turns can damage the delicate ensemble performance required to portray human contingency and incompleteness, and on that level this production sometimes feels more like a collection of exquisitely rendered individual performances – the human equivalent of the autumn leaves falling in its opening scene – than a true ensemble piece. There’s still much to admire. Sarks emphasises humiliation as key to whatever self-awareness the characters might avoid or achieve, and the romantic excruciations (everyone is famously in love with the wrong person) are beautifully done.

Advertisement

Philippa Northeast invests the role of Sonya with girlish comedy, throwing herself at Astrov (Fayssal Bazzi) with the full cringe of unrequited infatuation, while the charismatic doctor and environmentalist – whose dashing good looks and vaulting idealism coexist with burnout and radical disillusionment and emotional disconnection – seduces the beautiful young Yelena (Catherine Văn-Davies) with a palpable edge of self-loathing. Daniel Henshall’s Vanya is a veritable humiliation magnet. It’s a notably unsympathetic portrayal. A beta male to the core, this Vanya is an intensely pathetic figure who projects his own inadequacies onto his brother-in-law, the Professor (played in a nimble, lightly drawn lampoon of intellectual pomposity by Shaun Micallef) even as he makes embarrassing moves on the Professor’s young wife and pours blatant misogyny over everyone, including his would-be suffragist mother (Carolyn Bock). Daniel Henshall’s Vanya is a veritable humiliation magnet. Pia Johnson Vanya might feel like a minor character in his own life, but it’s Chekhov’s actual minor characters who cope best with humiliation. The longsuffering Waffles (Don Bridges) is warmly and affectionately conveyed, as is the stolidity of the pipe-smoking Nanny (Evelyn Krape). They’re both gloriously unselfconscious – one antidote to humiliation – and such brief moments of freedom are among the production’s most elevating, including a poignant scene where Sonya and Yelena are together, chatting and drinking and playing together like sisters, away from all the fuss the men are causing.

Advertisement

On opening night, some performances didn’t seem entirely bedded down. Henshall appeared to go dry at one point – a metatheatrical humiliation that seemed apposite, in context – but it might be the consistency of dramatic tempo that’s the biggest niggle. Related Article Streaming It may offend the book’s rusted-on fans, but this series should be approached with an open mind How we experience time, and how we handle futility and ennui, are among Chekhov’s main themes, and the one time I saw the Russians perform Vanya – by the Maly Drama Theatre of St Petersburg in 2007 – they brazenly manipulated the elastic temporal quality of theatre. (That production went for over three hours, dared the audience to be bored, and unfolded as inescapably as if it were being performed inside a black hole.) It would be churlish – maybe even Vanya-like – to complain that the audience wasn’t bored enough, though, and if it doesn’t quite deliver the epiphany into the human condition you get from the highest level of Chekhovian performance, this production’s desire to entertain is a no less crucial element of the drama. After all, Chekhov’s characters are always performing to allay such tedium, or at least give it form. And that aspect of being human is as timeless as it gets.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead

Advertisement

MUSIC

Silversun Pickups ★★★★

Forum Melbourne, July 28 When Silversun Pickups walk onto the stage at the Forum, they immediately get to work creating an immersive sonic atmosphere. Not a word is spoken until five songs in, when singer Brian Aubert finally addresses the crowd. Silversun Pickups perform at Forum Melbourne, July 28, 2026. Richard Clifford “Long time no see,” he says. “Since we were last in Melbourne [in 2012], the world fixed itself.” The audience titters. “Just kidding,” Aubert continues, smiling wryly. “It’s all f---ed up, [but] that’s outside these walls … Whatever ectoplasm and debris you’ve been coated in from our so-called leaders, in here, do your best to shake that shit off the best you can.” Indeed, the show is a sensory escape. The Los Angeles rock band’s ’90s-inspired soundscapes, incorporating elements of dream-pop, shoegaze and grunge, come to life on stage, accompanied by dappled lights swirling on the venue’s grand facade. From Aubert’s opening vocals on New Wave, the intensity grows, culminating in Nikki Monninger’s undulating bass, Christopher Guanlao’s thrashing drums and Joe Lester’s keys, collectively so heavy that the floor shakes and vibrates.

Advertisement

The band’s seventh album, Tenterhooks, was released in February, but there were a few more released in the years since they last graced our shores. Still, the bulk of the set is drawn from the new record and fan favourites Carnavas (2006) and Swoon (2009), with only a smattering of songs from the intervening years. After 25 years together, the band is a well-oiled machine, most evident on evocative tracks such as Three Seed, which showcase their ability to build an all-encompassing wall of sound. Nikki Monninger is magnetic as a bassist Richard Clifford Aubert’s distinctive voice has lost none of its sheen. Self-effacing, he jokes about how fans showed up to the now-defunct Ding Dong Lounge for the band’s debut Melbourne headliner in 2007 to see “that girl who sings”. “Surprise,” he deadpans, before performing early track Kissing Families. Monninger and Aubert sing together effortlessly on Panic Switch, but when she takes the lead for Au Revoir Reservoir, her vocals struggle to stay on-key. There’s less power in these moments, but Monninger is magnetic as a bassist, moving with ease and passion as she drives the songs forward. There are few bells and whistles at a Silversun Pickups show – it’s all about losing yourself in the sound, forgetting that anything and everything else exists for a little while. As Aubert sings on the band’s dreamlike signature track Lazy Eye, which closes the night, “It’s the room, the sun and the sky.”

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen

Advertisement

MUSIC

From Winter’s Stillness ★★★★

Australian Chamber Orchestra, Hamer Hall, until July 27 What do you get when you cross the Australian Chamber Orchestra with a jazz trumpeter and a Norwegian trio of female voices specialising in medieval, Nordic folk and contemporary music? Trumpeter Arve Henriksen performs is performing with the Australian Chamber Orchestra. Julia Marie Naglestad Well, certainly an edgy musical hybrid pushing the boundaries of “classical” programming, delighting intrepid listeners and probably perplexing others. The perplexity was heightened because printed programs only became available at interval, leaving most of the audience adrift in the unusual musical terrain of the first half. Trumpeter Arve Henriksen’s The Plume of Ash and Acceptance set a reflective mood, contrasted by the indefatigable minimalism of Terry Riley’s Half Wolf Dances Mad in the Moonlight.

Advertisement

Estonian composer Tõnu Kõrvits’ Bells, written for Henriksen and Trio Mediæval (singers Anna Maria Friman, Ditte Marie Bræin and Jorunn Lovise Husan), exerted a mesmeric quality that sat well alongside Academy Award-winning Icelandic composer Hildur Guðnadóttir’s Time and Water (especially written for this tour). Related Article ★★★★★

Melbourne live reviews It took 48 years, but this show has finally made it to Melbourne. It was worth the wait This Little Child, a sad traditional Norwegian song preceded Icelandic band Sigur Ros’ Fljótavik, an ideal vehicle for Hendriksen, whose unique, mellow tone unfurled over the music’s ground bass. In the second half, movements of Soviet composer Alfred Schnittke’s Concerto Grosso No.1 were interleaved with jazz-infused musings on Nordic chant and folk material. Schnittke’s iconoclasm is mercifully leavened with a generous sense of humour. Soloists Richard Tognetti and Satu Vänskä met the outrageous technical demands with aplomb, aided by customarily fine support from the rest of the ACO.

Advertisement

Using a cyclorama against which performers were either silhouetted or spotlit, head of lighting Joe Cox created a welcoming, unifying mood across this diverse program. Trio Mediæval’s limpid vocal quality was a delight throughout and together with flashes of brilliance from Henriksen, this eclectic experience was bound to get listeners talking – presumably as the ACO intended.

title: How to check your offset account is working properly after $55 million error exposed
text:
IN BRIEF A review by ASIC found banks paid over $55 million in customer compensation for offset account failures.

Experts said Australians should check whether their offset account has been set up and managed correctly.

Australians have lost millions of dollars to offset account errors, according to a review by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC).

The corporate regulator analysed the offset practices of eight banks, which it said represent more than 70 per cent of Australia's $2.5 trillion home loan market.

It found weaknesses in how all banks established, monitored and managed offset accounts.

Reports to ASIC between September 2023 and August 2025 showed that banks paid over $55 million in customer compensation for offset account failures.

In some cases, customers were repaid over $17,000 due to system limitations or administrative errors.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

What exactly is an offset account?

Offset accounts operate like everyday transaction accounts, which can be used to deposit and withdraw money. But they're often marketed as a simple way to reduce home loan interest.

That's because money held in an offset account also reduces the outstanding amount owed on a home loan, which is used to calculate the interest paid on that loan.

If a person has $50,000 in their offset account and a $750,000 loan, they will only be charged interest on $700,000.

Sally Tindall, director of data insights at Canstar, said offset accounts are a popular choice for many Australian mortgage holders.

"For many customers, it's one of the most powerful tools borrowers have to reduce the amount of interest they pay on their mortgage — but only if it's working as intended."

However, offset accounts are often associated with higher interest rates, additional account fees or a combination of both.

Check your offset account is linked

ASIC encouraged Australians to check whether their offset account was actually set up following their initial request.

Information about offset accounts should be available via a bank's mobile app, online banking or bank statements.

Some bank sites have mortgage offset pages which outline whether a person is eligible for an offset and how to find their account number.

ASIC's report also warned that refinancing or switching home loan products could break the link between an offset account and a person's mortgage.

In just over a month, a customer paid more than $3,500 in additional interest because their offset account was not linked, ASIC found.

Tindall said: "When you've spent years building up savings in your offset, the last thing you want is for those dollars to be sitting in an account that's not actually reducing your interest bill."

"But don't stop there, do some quick maths to make sure the interest you're being charged is on the amount you actually owe, factoring in the offset balance."

What to do if something looks wrong

Customers with complaints or questions should contact their bank directly.

According to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), if a person formally raises a complaint with their bank, they must respond within 21 days for complaints involving financial difficulty or 30 days for other issues.

If a person is not satisfied with their result, they can escalate the matter to AFCA, which will act as an independent mediator at no charge.

Under the Code of Banking Practice, banks have procedures in place to deal with and resolve complaints. Source: AAP

Kathy Tannous, an economics professor at Western Sydney University, told SBS News customers can take small steps to improve their financial literacy and understanding about their offset account.

She said people should "constantly review" their home loan statements and loan repayment schedules.

"I know these days it is a lot harder because there are many branches that are closed. It's also much harder to talk to an individual because we've got lovely chatbots and so on.

"But I would say, be persistent, because the time that you're spending on this may actually save you quite a bit of money."

title: The new plan to prevent data centres from driving power prices up
text:
In brief A new plan would force data centres to invest in renewable energy.

There are fears the power-hungry data centres could cause price hikes for electricity.

Large-scale data centres will be forced to invest in additional renewable energy to fuel their operations and avoid causing power price hikes in regulations agreed to by all but two states and territories.

The Energy and Climate Change Ministerial Council revealed its plans late on Tuesday after meeting to discuss advice on the issue from the Australian Energy Market Commission.

Climate groups welcomed the announcement and boost for renewable energy, but an organisation representing data centre operators warned the policy could be counterproductive if designed without their input.

The changes come weeks after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced plans to require data centres to be powered by clean energy projects under a shake-up of artificial intelligence rules, and after a NSW data centre inquiry heard similar calls for action.

The council, which includes energy ministers from the federal government and all state and territory governments, met virtually to discuss data centre energy proposals after flagging the issue in May.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

All ministers except those from Queensland and the Northern Territory agreed to pursue regulations that would "mandate that data centres offset their electricity demand by investing in additional renewable generation", the meeting communique said.

Renewable energy would need to be generated near the data centre unless local authorities opted out of the requirement, and the rules would be set at a national level, although states and territories could add additional requirements.

Changes to national rules would be considered in September, including reforms to the way data centres reported energy use.

The Climate Council called the proposed changes encouraging, although chief executive Amanda McKenzie said the rules should give data centre operators strict deadlines.

Governments from all Australian states and territories should also support the changes, she said, to avoid penalising some consumers with rising power bills.

"Unless these hold-out governments get on board, Queenslanders and Territorians will be left paying higher power bills, and we will all pay the price of higher climate pollution," she said.

But introducing a blanket rule for data centres' energy use could be ineffective if it was not designed with industry input, Data Centres Australia chief executive Belinda Dennett said.

Each centre operated differently to meet customer demands and use renewable energy, she told attendees at the Australian Clean Energy Summit, and removing options could produce poor results or deter investments.

"A one-size-fits-all approach will not work and may well be counterproductive to renewable energy investment objectives," Dennett said.

"The risk of removing this flexibility and taking a one-size-fits-all approach to energy procurement and offset arrangements may have consequences for how the data centre sector approaches renewable energy, and it's why good policy design matters and why industry needs to be at the table."

In Brief Australia contributed the lion's share of funding to Pacific nations in need of aid in 2024, a new report has found.

China has changed its strategy from major loans to smaller, strategic forms of aid in recent years.

Australia has continued to outrank China as the Pacific's biggest source of development aid, contributing a third of loans and infrastructure investment to the region, according to a new report.

Looking at development projects across the Pacific between 2008 and 2024, the Lowy Institute report found that, after years of decline, aid to the region increased by 10 per cent in 2024.

Total development aid stood at US$4.1 billion ($5.85 billion) in that year, but the report's authors estimate that would drop to US$3.8 billion ($5.42 billion) in yet-to-be-released 2025 figures.

With China now shifting strategy from big debt-fuelled loans to smaller strategic aid, and amid major economic shocks in the Pacific, the contest for regional influence is coming under greater strain.

Australia was the Pacific's biggest donor in 2024, giving $2.14 billion in aid, which made up 37 per cent of all finance to the region in that year.

A total of $6 billion in financing was dispensed from New Zealand, China, and regional development banks.

Australia has also inked $3.4 billion in loan deals, ending China's reign as the region's leading lender.

"That's a product of many years of Australia pushing into these spaces, but it's meant that what was once a real foothold for China in the region has been narrowed," the report's lead author Riley Duke told SBS News.

"Australia is consistently providing the most grant financing to the region, and that picture hasn't really changed."

Australia provided just over $US1.5 billion ($2.14 billion) across three sources of bilateral support to the Pacific in 2024.

The report, released on Tuesday, says demand for Chinese loans has dropped since 2019 due to concerns about servicing the debt, more competition between lenders and Chinese banks' capital availability.

Australia is also a major financier of climate change mitigation projects in the Pacific, including a solar and battery storage facility for Palau to help generate 20 per cent of its electricity, and Tonga's Renewable Energy Stabilisation Package.

The fruits of those efforts have paid off for Australia, with a flurry of regional security deals announced in recent months, including with Fiji, Vanuatu, Papua New Guinea and Tuvalu.

"They are a clear marker of Australia establishing itself as the lead partner to the region," Duke said.

"Those deals ... take a long time to progress. They're complicated, but they reflect Australia establishing itself as an inalienably important partner to Pacific countries."

Why does the Pacific rely on aid?

Developing Pacific Island nations have been hit hard by multiple shocks, including the COVID-19 pandemic and more recently, fuel supply shortages caused by the United States-Israeli war on Iran.

Duke said these multiple challenges put the region at risk of a "lost decade" of development, with Pacific economies caught in "a continual cycle of shock and recovery".

Food and importing oil costs much more for the Pacific than other countries because of transport fees, fertiliser prices and reliance on diesel generators for power.

READ MORE Australia is courting its next Pacific partner

The war on Iran is estimated to hit Pacific economic growth, shaving 1 per cent off pre-war growth projections of 3.4 per cent next year.

Australia has stepped in to help Fiji, Solomon Islands, and Samoa to help absorb fuel-price shocks and help with supply.

What is China helping build in the Pacific?

China used to be the dominant lender to the region but shifted its strategy in more recent years to focus on more "small and beautiful" projects — as President Xi Jinping has described it — to win regional influence.

"China's lending collapse to the region, sort of meant that it had to pivot or adapt how it engaged through aid and development channels, and how that's materialised is these smaller, more grassroots projects," Duke said.

"China is offering more training. It's been donating more equipment, more scholarships, and you know it's trying to find new ways to build relationships with Pacific countries."

Those smaller donations include equipment to schools, police forces, and hospitals across the Pacific, as well as training to build up regional health, media, and policing industries.

Its largest single grant is a US$135 million ($192.63 million) project for new roads and bridges in Fiji, followed by the Nauru National Sports Stadium (US$73 million), the Vanuatu Earthquake Recovery Grant (US $57 million), and the High School Sports Complex in Tonga (US$26 million).

Duke said Chinese aid in the Pacific is "highly reactive" to diplomatic developments, and acts as a "strategic lever".

"When a country switches diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing, or opens strategic negotiations with Australia, Chinese aid flows react."

One example is Nauru's 2024 switch of diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing — after which a flurry of Chinese aid followed, including the stadium project.

The report also found Chinese state-owned firms dominate contracts for infrastructure projects, including for multilateral projects.

title: 'Hidden harm': The $17k offset account failure that exposes banks' costly blind spot
text:
IN BRIEF A report by ASIC has found that some banks failed to deliver promises on offset account savings.

The Australian Banking Association said banks take any identified issues very seriously and have compensated customers impacted.

Offset accounts are often marketed as a simple way to reduce home loan interest, but a report by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) has found that some banks fail to deliver on that promise.

ASIC, Australia's financial services and consumer credit regulator, reviewed the offset practices of eight banks, which together represent more than 70 per cent of Australia's approximately $2.5 trillion home loan market.

It found that, while practices varied across these financial institutions — AMP, ANZ, CommBank, Great Southern Bank, HSBC Australia, ING, Macquarie Bank and Westpac — there were weaknesses in how they established, monitored and managed offset accounts.

It identified two cases where customers unknowingly paid more than $17,000 extra interest on their home loan because the bank did not make clear that offset accounts had to be re-linked after refinancing.

In another circumstance, a customer paid over $3,500 in additional interest over about a month after their account was incorrectly de-linked.

Reports to ASIC between 1 September 2023 and 31 August 2025 showed banks paid more than $55 million in customer compensation for offset account failures.

It expects compensation to continue as banks further analyse offset account operations.

ASIC chair Sarah Court said that "when offset accounts don't operate correctly, the harm can be hidden".

"Loan repayments stay the same, while customers unknowingly pay more interest and take longer to repay their loan."

What is an offset account?

Hue Hwa Au Yong, a senior lecturer in banking and finance at Monash University, said offset accounts are "simple to understand but difficult for customers to verify".

Like an everyday transaction account, offset accounts can be used to deposit and withdraw money.

However, the amount of money in an offset account also reduces the outstanding amount owed on a home loan, which is used to calculate interest.

If a person has $50,000 in their offset account and a $750,000 loan, they will only be charged interest on $700,000.

"So, the issue really is not the product itself, but the system behind it," Yong told SBS News.

"As a bank customer, we can see how much money is in our offset account. But as a borrower, we can't easily verify whether the banking systems are correctly applying it when calculating interest, [which] ... is calculated daily using a quite complex formula and system. "

Australian Banking Association CEO Simon Birmingham told SBS News that offset accounts "can be an effective way for mortgage holders to save on interest and in more than 99 per cent of cases banks were found to manage them correctly".

He said banks had "already taken action to compensate the small number of customers where those banks identified errors, often manual errors".

Offset accounts in Australia

As of March this year, Australians had almost $350 billion in offset accounts, a 28 per cent increase over the past two years, according to ASIC.

Kathy Tannous — a professor in economics at Western Sydney University's Business School — said offset accounts are becoming increasingly popular.

"Around 40 per cent of all mortgage holders use an offset account according to recent research," Tannous told SBS News.

"Part of the appeal is twofold in Australia: our level of housing ownership but also the size of our mortgages — the amount we have to borrow relative to our income in order to buy what we call the 'Australian dream' of owning a property".

Offset accounts are an increasingly popular option for many mortgage holders in Australia. Source: Getty / Ingrid_Hendriksen

However, offset accounts are also associated with higher interest rates, additional account fees or a combination of both.

Offset accounts are not available in the United States due to tax regulations. They are an option in New Zealand and the United Kingdom, but are less common than in Australia.

Customers 'doubly hit'

According to ASIC's report, there are several key reasons why banks have "insufficient oversight and inadequate responses" to customers regarding offset accounts.

The regulator found some banks "struggled" to readily identify if or when customers had requested an offset account.

It also alleged banks were unaware they were failing to deliver on promises for offset accounts.

It claims some financial institutions were slow to fix issues, compensate customers and didn't provide easily accessible online information.

Court said that, when offset account failures occur, "customers are doubly hit" — not only losing promised interest savings but also the opportunity to use that money elsewhere.

The report also provides examples of "more positive action by banks", including improvements to offset practices before and during the review.

Some banks have committed to make changes after ASIC's reporting, according to the regulator.

Calls for change?

Tannous believes in Australia, some people rely on banks, "almost like you're relying on your doctor to treat you medically".

"You rely on banks to treat you financially. That they will provide you with information in a way that you can understand it and make a decision."

She described ASIC's report as "most concerning" but acknowledged the regulator's findings were limited to a two-year period.

ASIC has called for greater transparency from banks to amend what it has described as weaknesses in offset account practices. That includes information about offset accounts on bank websites and mobile apps.

Yong said the onus should be on banks, not customers, to detect errors in offset accounts but also encouraged Australians to be "proactive" and contact their bank if they had concerns.

Birmingham also said "banks take any identified issues very seriously, with these banks already compensating their customers and taking steps to further strengthen their offset account practices".

title: Gina Rinehart funded flights and fashion show for Pauline Hanson
text:
IN BRIEF Pauline Hanson didn't disclose how the bill was split but remained adamant "not one cent" of taxpayer money was used.

The pair holidayed in Europe in mid-July, attending a luxury fashion show and staying at a luxury Italian resort.

Mining magnate Gina Rinehart flew One Nation leader Pauline Hanson around Europe and paid for her tickets to a luxury fashion show while she was there.

Hanson's flights from London to Sicily via Rome, and back again, were all funded by Rinehart, the senator's parliamentary register of interests revealed after being updated on Tuesday.

However, Hanson reported paying for accommodation, meals and daily expenses herself during the trip, which took place between 11 and 16 July, as first reported by Fairfax outlets.

Hanson drew criticism after she and Rinehart were sighted at a luxury Italian resort and attending a Dolce and Gabbana fashion event in Sicily.

Questioned when she returned to Australia, Hanson did not go into detail on how the bill was split, but insisted taxpayers had not paid for the luxury weekend.

title: Australia has a favourite day to say 'I do' — but fewer couples are saying it
text:
In brief New Australian Bureau of Statistics data reveals 25 October was the most popular wedding date last year.

It also found the marriage rate continued to decline, and the divorce rate ticked up for the first time in years.

Saturday 25 October was Australia's favourite day to say "I do" in 2025 — but new data suggests fewer couples are saying it.

Fewer Australians tied the knot last year than the year before, according to new figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

At the same time, more marriages are coming to an end, with the divorce rate ticking upward for the first time in several years, though ultimately remaining lower than it was 20 years ago.

The most popular day to get hitched

The most popular wedding date in 2025 was Saturday 25 October — i.e. the symmetrical 25/10/25 — with 2,035 marriages.

That's about 500 more than the runner-up, Saturday 22 November (22/11/25) — which had 1,527.

ABS data show there's somewhat of a trend towards more marriages on dates with numerical significance, though for some it could also be coincidence.

The least popular days were Christmas Day, with 51 weddings, Boxing Day with 54, New Year's Day with 57, and Tuesday 29 July with 61.

Spring dominated the wedding calendar, with most of the top ten dates falling in September, October and November. The rest were scattered across autumn.

Last year, 25/10/25 was the most popular date for Australians to tie the knot. Source: SBS News

Saturday remains, unsurprisingly, the nation's preferred wedding day — more than 52,000 marriages took place on a Saturday in 2025, and 45 of the year's most popular dates fell on one.

Friday came in second, with just over 21,000 marriages, led by Friday 10 October (10/10/25).

Zoom out further, and one day still reigns supreme: 10 November 2012 — the sequential 10/11/12.

That remains the most popular wedding date of the past 20 years, with 3,081 marriages recorded on that day — still comfortably ahead of the runner-up, 11 November 2011 (11/11/11), which had 2,614.

Fewer couples tying the knot

Beyond the calendar quirks, the broader numbers tell a clearer story: marriage is becoming less common in Australia.

There were 118,804 marriages registered in 2025 — 2,040 fewer than in 2024, a drop of 1.7 per cent.

That's in line with 2023's total (118,439), but still well above the pandemic-era lows of 2020 and 2021.

Adjusted for population, the marriage rate — the number of marriages per 1,000 people aged 16 and over — fell slightly to 5.3 in 2025, down from 5.5 in both 2023 and 2024.

Zoom out to 2005, where the marriage rate was 6.9, and the decline is even more stark.

The biggest drops came among 25-29 and 30-34 year-olds. No age group recorded an increase.

In the last 20 years, Australia's marriage rate has declined — but so has the proportion of people getting divorced. Source: SBS News

Despite the falling numbers, the age at which Australians marry has barely moved: 32.7 years for men (down marginally from 32.8 in 2024) and 31.2 years for women, unchanged for the third year running.

Same-sex and non-binary marriages held steady too, making up 3.9 per cent of all marriages for a third consecutive year. More marriages were between two women (2,527) than two men (1,849).

More couples calling it quits

On the other side of the ledger, 49,158 divorces were granted in 2025, a 4.1 per cent rise on 2024's 47,216.

That brings the total roughly back in line with 2022 levels (49,241).

The divorce rate — divorces per 1,000 people aged 16 and over — rose to 2.2, up from 2.1 in 2024.

But the bigger picture across two decades reveals fewer people are getting divorced: in 2005, the divorce rate was 3.3 per 1,000 people, compared to 2025's 2.2 figure.

READ MORE Kate says her cancer led to divorce. The aftermath of it was even more surprising

Australians are also divorcing slightly later in life: the median age at divorce rose to 47.3 years for men and 44.4 for women, both up marginally on 2024.

But marriages that do end are lasting longer before couples separate — a median of 9.4 years in 2025, up from 9.3 the year before.

That data suggests Australians may be walking down the aisle less often each year, but marriages may be proving more durable than they were two decades ago.

title: Origin apologises after revealing 900,000 customers affected by data breach
text:
In Brief Origin says 900,000 customers were affected by a data breach.

It's advising customers to be wary of a heightened risk of scammers.

Almost one million Origin Energy customers had their details accessed by hackers after a major data breach last week, the company has revealed.

On Tuesday, Origin said it had completed an initial review into the incident and identified that approximately 900,000 current and former customers' data was accessed by the hackers.

"To our customers, I am sorry. We don't take for granted the trust customers place in Origin and our safeguarding of their information," CEO Frank Calabria said in a statement.

Last week, the energy company announced it was the victim of the security incident, saying names, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers and account information could all have been viewed.

Other potential details include the last four digits of credit cards, or the last three digits of bank accounts.

The company said it would be contacting affected customers first and was opening up a dedicated hotline for those concerned.

Origin said it had been trying to confirm the credibility of the threat since early July.

"We worked to confirm its credibility and potential impact; however, based on the information available, it was not assessed to be credible," Calabria said.

READ MORE Origin Energy reports customer bank, credit card details caught up in data breach

"On 22 July, new information emerged that indicated a potential security incident may have occurred. We acted immediately, providing updates to the market and notifying our customers as a precaution."

Origin, which has 4.8 million customer accounts in Australia and provides electricity, natural gas, LPG and internet services, said last week it did not believe the data obtained included credit card or bank details.

Customers advised to be wary of scams

The company has also warned customers to be alert to a greater risk of scams that could arise from the data breach, advising customers to be wary of unexpected calls, emails or texts referring to their account.

Those who get such contact should independently contact Origin through numbers on official channels, it said, and do not provide passwords or personal information to anyone.

"We are acutely aware that others may exploit this incident, including by impersonating Origin or through other scam activity," Calabria said.

"We recommend that all our customers remain vigilant to suspicious activity and a heightened risk of scams.

Griffith University's Graeme Hughes, an expert on business and consumer issues, said the breach was unlikely to cause cases of payment fraud but marked a "social engineering problem".

"The last four digits for a card, a date of birth, and an authentic billing history are the exact trust signals a business uses to verify itself over the phone," Hughes told the Australian Associated Press.

"That makes an unsolicited call about an energy account far more convincing than it should be.

— With additional reporting by the Australian Associated Press.

title: 'I'm not Jacinta Allan': Caroll pledges 'new direction' and calls a royal commission
text:
In Brief Jacinta Allan announced her resignation shortly before a party room meeting that would have seen a leadership spill.

Deputy Premier Ben Carroll was elected to the tob job after a lengthy, chaotic meeting.

New Victorian Premier Ben Carroll has declared he will lead his government in a "new direction", while distancing himself from his predecessors Jacinta Allan and Daniel Andrews.

In his first comments after being elected state Labor leader, Carroll also announced a royal commission into the construction sector, which has been marred by corruption allegations, and the strengthening of Victoria's anti-corruption watchdog.

Allan had consistently rejected calls for an inquiry.

"Let me make one thing very clear: I am not Daniel Andrews. I am not Jacinta Allan," he said on Tuesday afternoon, just hours after Allan's resignation.

"I will do things differently, because different times require a new approach.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"In my government, integrity will not be optional."

The former deputy premier said "circumstances changed" in the six weeks since he promised Allan he would not challenge her for the top job. He thanked Allan for her service to the Labor Party and the state.

Carroll was elected to the top job after a chaotic party room meeting triggered by Allan's resignation, following her loss of party support amid dire polling.

Polls showed voters are frustrated with the high cost of living, rising state debt, infrastructure delays and alleged corruption on the state's Big Build projects.

Carroll was expected to secure the leadership unopposed before Victorian Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny mounted a late challenge.

Under Labor rules, a contested leadership ballot must be put to a vote of the party's rank-and-file members.

The process could take weeks and would plunge the government into political instability just months before the November state election.

But after a lengthy meeting, during which both yelling and cheering could be heard at various stages, Carroll emerged as premier. State Transport Minister Gabrielle Williams was elected his deputy.

'Honour of my life'

Announcing her resignation on Tuesday morning, Allan said it had been an honour to serve as leader.

"The most important thing I want to say today is thank you," Allan said.

"Thank you to the Victorian people. It has been the honour of my life to serve you as your premier. I stepped down after 1,036 days in this role. Not one of them wasted, not one of them easy."

Allan said she believed she would have won a rank-and-file membership vote, but said the process would have been damaging in the lead-up to the November election.

"More importantly, it puts the state in a position of uncertainty. That hurts the Victorian people, and I just won't do that. At the end of the day, I am, and always have been, a team player."

Allan reflected on her nearly three years as premier, saying her biggest priority had been tackling the cost of living.

"Making life easier and more affordable became my mission," she said.

"We not only made public transport free during a fuel crisis, we made public transport free for kids forever.

"We cut car rego for three and a half million people, and we doubled food relief so families could have the dignity of a meal. And we're making working from home a right that your boss can't take away."

Allan held back tears as she spoke about women's health, reflecting on her own experience with endometriosis and nearly losing her own daughter during birth.

"I led a government that listened to girls about their health," she said.

"We opened 15 women's health clinics across the state. We've rolled out the green whistle for pain relief free of charge, and you can get the pill at the chemist without having to pay to see a GP."

Allan said she would have "absolutely relished the fight" ahead of the November election as she delivered a parting warning to her successor.

"I was more than ready. I saw off two Liberal leaders," she said.

"I expect my successor will see off the third. And if they don't, One Nation certainly will."

Allan, who was elected the state's youngest-ever female MP at the age of 25 in 1999, said she hoped more women entered politics.

"Please don't look at what I have experienced this week and think, 'Stuff that. I don't want to be involved,'" she said.

"Look at the support I've experienced over my career, and think, 'I can make a difference here too.'"

The looming election comes as polling suggests support for the state Labor government has collapsed in recent months.

The party had been campaigning for a fourth consecutive term against the rising popularity of One Nation.

title: Iran claims control of the Strait of Hormuz and rejects peace talks
text:
IN BRIEF Trump ended a two-week bombing campaign against Iran after advice they were running out of targets.

Iran has rejected peace talks as the US struggles to break the nation's control of the strait.

Iran says it is still in control of the Strait of Hormuz and not ‌seeking to resume peace talks with the United States.

Following 13 successive nights of intensifying bombing that provoked Iran to fire ‌on US bases in response, Trump halted the campaign over the weekend.

Iran said it would pause its own attacks for as long as the US pause in bombing endures.

Trump's decision to suspend the campaign reflected advice from his top brass ‌that the bombing, aimed at breaking Iran's grip on the strait, had reached the limits of what it could achieve, according to a US official and widespread US media reports.

The US official told Reuters that military commanders had advised the president they were running out of targets.

The official said the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Dan Caine, had also expressed concern over the depletion of air defence weapons used to protect US bases in the region.

Similar reports indicating that civilian and military aides had advised Trump to halt the campaign were carried over the weekend by the New York Times, CNN, Axios and other news outlets.

The US ambassador to the United Nations, Mike Waltz, said on ‌Sunday Trump had paused ‌the campaign to allow room for negotiations.

But ⁠the spokesperson for Iran's Foreign Ministry, Esmail Baghaei, said in a televised press conference on Monday that Iran had not asked to resume peace talks with the United States.

The end of the US bombing campaign sent oil prices tumbling in the hope that disrupted global supplies could resume flowing.

Brent crude, which had briefly ticked above AU$150 a barrel last week for the first time since May, fell around 7.8 per cent by mid-morning on Monday to just under AU$130.

But in a clear bid to signal that the US bombing had failed in its objective, Tehran indicated it was still in control of the world's most important waterway for energy markets.

Several Iranian state media outlets carried the same report, citing an "informed source" as saying that Iran had turned around six "offending ships" on Monday morning that had attempted to cross the strait without ⁠its permission.

READ MORE Israeli settlers torch two mosques in West Bank during a deadly surge in violence

"As previously announced, the traffic route in the Strait ‌of Hormuz is the route specified by Iran, and other routes are contaminated and have no way out," the Iranian state media reports quoted the source as saying.

Trump launched his renewed bombing campaign to punish Iran after Tehran fired on ships using a route through the strait that ‌has been promoted by the United States, which has told vessels to sail close to the coast of Oman.

Iran says ships may pass only through a channel that runs closer to its own coast, which it controls and where it intends to impose transit fees.

The two weeks of renewed US bombing killed scores of people in Iran and destroyed bridges and tunnels across the south as well as military targets.

Four US service members were killed by Iran's return fire against US bases in neighbouring Arab states. Iran also struck civilian infrastructure in Gulf countries in what it said was retaliation for US strikes on civilian targets.

The ‌halt to the renewed US bombing campaign leaves no clear indication of what leverage the US can exert to achieve Trump's aim to break Iran's grip on the strait.

The US and Iran reached an agreement in June on a framework for talks meant to take place by the end of August to resolve major issues such as Iran's nuclear program.

READ MORE US and Iran halt bombing for second night as both sides give space to talks

But the sides have disputed the meaning of the memorandum's language about the Strait of Hormuz, with the US insisting it requires Iran to allow free travel while Iran says it grants it the authority to supervise transit.

Iran aims to formalise its control over the strait by reaching an agreement with Oman, which controls the opposite shore. A senior Omani delegation was in Tehran over the weekend discussing the future of the strait.

The foreign ministers of Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia each had held phone calls to discuss the strait with Oman's Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi, according to reports on Monday on Qatari, UAE and Saudi state ⁠media.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who launched the war in February alongside Trump but has not participated in the US-Iranian negotiations to end it, is due to meet Trump in Washington early this week.

title: The green light is on for tax returns. One thing won't get your refund faster
text:
IN BRIEF The ATO has loaded a vast amount of data into its systems to make lodging tax returns easier and more accurate.

The ATO uses data matching to detect incorrect claims and may delay refunds while suspicious returns are checked.

The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) says taxpayers with straightforward tax affairs can now begin lodging their tax returns, with most income statements and pre-fill information now available.

More than 100 million pieces of data from employers, banks, private health insurers, share registries and government agencies have been loaded into the ATO's systems to help people lodge more accurately and with less effort.

ATO assistant commissioner Anita Challen released a statement saying that most income statements and pre-fill information is now available.

"If you're self-lodging, before you hit submit, take a few extra minutes to check your details to avoid delays and mistakes," she said.

The ATO is also expanding its pre-fill services this year to include income reported through the Taxable Payment Annual Report.

From late August, contractors in some industries — including construction, cleaning, courier services, information technology, road freight and security — may see that income automatically added to their returns.

Do I have 'straightforward' tax affairs?

Your tax affairs are likely to be straightforward if you're primarily paying tax on salary and wages, with only a small amount of taxable investment income or government payments.

If you're applying for more than basic deductions, or your return includes elements like capital gains, receipt of rental payments and foreign income, your return may not be straightforward.

If you're unsure, you should consult a tax accountant or services such as the ATO's Tax Help or National Tax Clinic for advice.

Common mistakes taxpayers should avoid

The ATO is also warning Australians against overclaiming deductions or failing to declare all sources of income.

That includes earnings from side hustles, cash jobs, rental properties and online content creation.

The agency says it uses sophisticated data-matching systems to detect suspicious claims and may delay refunds while returns are investigated.

Taxpayers are also being urged not to simply copy deductions from previous years if their work or circumstances have changed.

The ATO is reminding Australians that the proposed $1,000 standard work-related deduction does not apply this tax time and cannot be claimed until the 2027 tax year.

It is also warning people not to rely on tax advice from artificial intelligence platforms, social media "finfluencers", family or friends without checking official guidance or speaking to a registered tax professional.

Before lodging, the ATO recommends taxpayers check their personal details, bank account and superannuation information are up to date and ensure all pre-filled information is accurate.

It also encourages people to keep records of deductions, use the ATO app to track their return and remain alert to scams.

The tax office says it will never send unsolicited messages containing links asking people to log in or provide personal information.

Most tax returns are processed within 12 business days, according to the ATO, which says calling the agency will not speed up the process.

People lodging their own tax return have until 31 October, while those using a registered tax agent may have longer, provided they are on their agent's books before that date.

City of Perth councillors have gone against staff recommendations and denied an adult store’s request to operate a sex-on-premises site in the heart of the city, suggesting they take it to Northbridge instead. While three elected members voted in support of the Pink Rabbit Club venue on Barrack Street operating as an LGBTQI+ community safe space, the vote on Tuesday night required an absolute majority and thus failed to get over the line. The building located at 129 Barrack Street, currently operates as an adult retail shop – known as Pink Rabbit Adult Boutique. Michael Philipps The development application sought to allow the Pink Rabbit Club to run an adults-only exclusive club for consensual sexual activities at 129 Barrack Street. Currently, the building operates as an adult retail shop – known as Pink Rabbit Adult Boutique – on the ground floor, but the development application would see the upper floor become a space for “social connection, education and consensual sexual activity”.

The report to council noted the applicant, Rowe Group, described the space as being designed to “foster a sex-positive, inclusive, and affirming environment for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, and other identities within the community”. “As an 18+ exclusive club, it emphasises social connection, education, and consensual intimate activities in a non-judgmental setting. Members are united by a shared interest in fostering LGBTQI+ community connections, including safe discussions, social interactions, and consensual activities (including those of sexual nature) that support personal expression and well-being,” the applicant said in the report. Speaking in favour of the venue, councillor Liam Gobbert said the proposal offered no reasons for objection. “Should the clientele be a factor in determining this matter, it would amount to an interference, I believe, in a landowner’s private enjoyment of their lot,” he said. “I do think it is worth mentioning, though, having said that, that the proposed clientele to being the LGBTQIA+ community is a good thing.

“Safe spaces for any historically or contemporaneously marginalised, disadvantaged, or persecuted parts of the community are a good thing, and that a private landowner is seeking to provide that type of a safe space in our city without government support should be seen as a good thing.” Related Article City life Perth CBD ‘sex-on-premise’ venue tipped for approval despite community backlash Councillor Lisa Ma, who also supported the proposal, said the council should respond directly to the concerns raised by the community about this item “because, underneath the language of location and antisocial behaviour, the real discomfort for many is the sex-on-premises nature of this venue”. “So on location, let’s be honest about what’s really being asked: not ‘is Barrack Street suitable’, but ‘should this kind of activity exist anywhere in our city at all?’,” she said. “Sex-on-premises venues aren’t exactly new or exotic. They operate lawfully across Australian capital cities, always as private membership-based clubs, and precisely because of that, that structure keeps the activity consensual, controlled, and out of the public view.

Advertisement

“Again, this proposal follows that exact model: upstairs, no signage, no street presence, members only. If we reject here on locational grounds, in my opinion, we’re not solving a planning problem. “We’re saying we’d rather this activity stay unregulated and out of sight somewhere we don’t have to think about.” Despite their championing for the approval, fellow council members were not prepared to budge. Councillor Catherine Lezer said there was a place for inclusive safe spaces in the city – but it was not on Barrack Street. “The submissions and the ratepayers tell me a venue for adult activity does not belong here,” she said.

“Barrack Street in 2026 is a vastly different place from the COVID-recovery vacancy landscape of 2022, when the Pink Rabbit retail-only store was approved. There are now shops, cafés, restaurants, family apartments, hotels, renovated heritage buildings, and Barrack Street continues to improve. “I urge the owner to perhaps consider Northbridge, an entertainment precinct suited for this type of venue. This is simply the wrong use in the wrong place.” Similarly, councillor Chris Patten said an entertainment precinct would be a “much better location” for a sex-on-premises site. Councillor Viktor Ko said one of his main concerns was that members would have to pay for a membership to attend the venue. “I cannot agree with charging for membership. It goes against the model of inclusion. It goes against the model of actually including and welcoming people,” he said.

Advertisement

“And from my research, I can’t find any other business in the city that actually offers the same service as this. So if we do approve this, this will be one of its one of its only businesses in the city that offers this.” Related Article Planning and development ‘Like a fishbowl’: Perth heritage precinct, mosque unite against eight-storey tower Gobbert warned that refusal of the development application could result in an expensive State Administrative Tribunal hearing. “I couldn’t see any [reasons] in this DA. Is there a legitimate reason to refuse the DA, and what’s the going rate for defending a SAT case at the moment? Is it $25,000 to $30,000 of ratepayers money?” he asked the council staff. Acting chief executive Maria Cooke said amenity impact claims were not strong enough to warrant a refusal, and that SAT rates, depending on the length of the hearing, could cost tens of thousands of dollars.

Advertisement

The recommendation to approve the sex-on-premises site was lost 4-3. Councillors Raj Doshi and Adam Pacan were absent from the meeting and therefore did not vote. Perth Lord Mayor Bruce Reynolds made an alternative motion to refuse the application because the venue would “adversely impact upon the amenity and character of the locality … by way of adverse noise, reduced public safety, and residential and social behaviour”. It was approved 5-2 with councillors Ma and Gobbert voting against it.

Patriot Resources has bolted on another slice of highly prospective ground in the heart Zambia’s world class copper belt, acquiring a 90 per cent interest in a strategic licence. The tenement sits just 17 kilometres along strike from First Quantum Minerals’ soon-to-be producing Fishtie project which is expected to ramp up to a production rate of about 30,000 tonnes of copper a year by the end of the decade. The company paid just US$50,000 (A$71,600) for its majority stake in the 16.15-square-kilometre licence, with US$20,000 (A$28,700) paid on signing and the balance due on completion. The vendor will be free-carried on the remaining 10 per cent interest. Patriot Resources has acquired a new licence in the Zambian Copperbelt, hosted in similar stratigraphy as Ivanhoe Mines giant Kamoa copper mine in the DRC. The new ground, located 12km north of Mkushi, is believed to cover the south-western extension of the Lusale Basin mineralised corridor – a significant geological feature which forms part of a neighbourhood that has hosted some of the largest copper deposits in the world. The basin is considered a satellite of the revered Central African copper belt that straddles the border between Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). For a junior explorer, securing ground with a geological address close to some of the world’s premier copper deposits represents a serious coup for this sub-$20m market cap company.

Advertisement

Patriot says the mineralisation style is hosted in a stratigraphic position that shares many similarities to what churned out Ivanhoe Mines’ colossal, 34 million tonnes of contained copper, Kamoa deposit in the DRC and the Lonshi deposit on the eastern flank of the Zambian Copperbelt. Patriot’s new tenement sits within the Katanga Supergroup, an approximately 7km-thick sequence of rocks that hosts the majority of the region’s prolific copper and cobalt deposits. The acquisition complements the company’s recent success at its Tonic prospect, within the Mumbwa project area also in Zambia. Maiden reverse circulation drilling at Tonic in early July confirmed notable copper-silver-zinc-cobalt mineralisation from surface. One hole delivered a solid 17 metre hit at 0.41 per cent copper, 4.7 grams per tonne (g/t) silver and 0.30 per cent zinc from 29m. That interval included a higher-grade core of 7 metres grading 0.78 per cent copper, 5.1g/t silver and 0.38 per cent zinc from 30m. Patriot says the Tonic system remains open at depth and along strike, with most of its defined induced polarisation, or “IP” footprint yet to feel the drill bit. The target corridor now steps out to the southeast from Tonic for a total distance of 5.5km. Importantly, the targets line up along the same northwest-southeast trending Mumbwa Fault Zone that hosts Sinomine Resource Group’s, 675,000 tonnes of contained copper, Kitumba deposit, a mere 18km from Tonic.

Advertisement

Notably, the nearby infrastructure angle adds further appeal to the address with The Kitumba development including a processing facility and copper smelter due for commissioning this year. Whilst copper in Zambia is clearly a major focus, Patriot is also advancing its impressive Tassa silver-gold play in Peru, where a recent re-assay program has successfully validated historical grades ahead of a planned maiden drill campaign. The validation is a critical step, as Tassa already features a JORC-compliant inferred resource of 31.4 million silver-equivalent ounces grading a solid 52.68 grams per tonne silver equivalent. The real blue sky was unveiled in May when Patriot blew out the project’s conceptual exploration target to a mammoth range of between 559 million and 774 million silver-equivalent ounces. The addition of a Zambian copper play looks to have completed a trifecta of near-term activity priorities for Patriot. A phase-two drill campaign at its Tonic copper discovery, geophysics and mapping at its newly acquired licence in Zambia, and a maiden drill program to test the scale of its Tassa silver project in Peru now all loom large. Additionally, Patriot continues its divestment strategy for its Gorman lithium project in Ontario, Canada, signalling a clear focus on its most promising assets in tier-one jurisdictions.

The company looks to have been to be picking up assets based on postcodes carefully. By securing ground with geological similarities to a world-beating deposit and located just down the road from a major player, Patriot has given itself a good chance of clocking a discovery. With drill rods set to turn in the coming months at Tassa and Tonic, and plenty of news flow to come, this ASX-junior is worth keeping an eye on. Traffic in the Sicilian capital of Palermo is notoriously chaotic. Lights there, at least in the popular imagination, are regarded as offering mere guidelines to motorists. “Court orders are not like the traffic lights in Palermo,” Justice Michael Lee said to a Sydney courtroom. “They are not there merely to be observed when it is thought convenient to do so.” Justice Michael Lee, who put Qantas to the rhetorical sword in an earlier judgment, rounded on lawyers representing its sacked workers. Marija Ercegovac And so on Wednesday, Lee slammed Maurice Blackburn, the law firm representing 1820 sacked Qantas workers, for failing to distribute $120 million owed to the workers by a July 31 deadline and asking him for more time. The firm would be in breach of court orders, Lee said, and he signalled potential punishments. Lee questioned why the delays “only became apparent in mid-June, despite issues developing over months”, and why he had not been informed earlier. “What ought not occur is that the court is presented, at one minute to midnight, with what was presented as a fait accompli,” Lee said.

He rejected the request by Maurice Blackburn to alter orders made last year that compensation for fired Qantas ground staff be completed by July 31, 2026 and scheduled a longer hearing on the matter for August 6. “You’ll be in breach of [the orders by then], and we’ll see what consequences flow from that,” Lee said, though he cautioned that the firm may have a good explanation for the delay. He suggested the court may need to change the process for at least part of the amount that workers are owed because he had “no confidence” that Maurice Blackburn’s process would be completed in a timely fashion. Related Article Aviation Alan Joyce has been writing his book. Here’s how five people illegally sacked by his airline have fared The more than 1800 former Qantas workers who were unlawfully sacked by the airline during the pandemic have been waiting for compensation for more than five years. Qantas has agreed to a $120 million compensation fund. Last year, Lee also imposed a further $90 million fine on Qantas, of which $40 million is to go to the employees. But only $5 million of the money has been paid so far, as Maurice Blackburn tries to calculate the financial and intangible loss suffered by each worker. That has infuriated the former workers, some of whom have accused the law firm of delaying the process with unnecessarily technical calculations and seeking years of documents some of the cohort don’t have.

The Transport Workers’ Union expressed hope that workers would soon be paid. The union had brought the case against Qantas in 2020 after the airline sacked the workers in part to stop them from exercising a legal right to take industrial action as they bargained for more pay. “These workers, backed by their union, won this case against all odds when not even the Coalition government was standing up to Qantas’ decision,” said TWU national secretary Michael Kaine. “Maurice Blackburn added its experience, having fought and won other significant worker cases. But now it needs to step up to deliver the compensation these workers deserve into their pockets,” Kaine said. Maurice Blackburn had no comment on the Wednesday hearing. It has previously told this masthead that its compensation effort involved about 40 people, including external experts, who had combed through more than 17,500 individual tax documents. It had also followed up directly with claimants where material was missing or incorrect to help them find it, the firm previously said.

text:

Key points THEATRE: Melbourne Theatre Company’s Uncle Vanya offers up sardonic one-liners

MUSIC: Silversun Pickups at the Forum is all about losing yourself in the sound

MUSIC: ACO’s From Winter’s Stillness is an edgy musical hybrid

THEATRE

Uncle Vanya ★★★★

Melbourne Theatre Company, Arts Centre Melbourne, until August 22 It’s a rare and charming thing to see Uncle Vanya done in period dress, as it is in Anne-Louise Sarks’ latest production for the MTC, on a splendid set that evokes a crumbling provincial estate in the last decade of the 19th century. Singling out actors for praise in Chekhov may be inevitable but always feels like a betrayal. Pia Johnson Contemporary Chekhovian performance tends to modernise, reframe, relocate. It’s as if we wanted to fire a bullet at the past – an exercise in futility, as Vanya himself discovers twice. Time doesn’t work that way. Playwright Joanna Murray-Smith believes (rightly) that such modernising is unnecessary in a good Chekhov production. Her Vanya adaptation gives a light textual massage for clarity, to draw out the comedy and update the vernacular.

Advertisement

As you’d expect from Murray-Smith, the sardonic one-liners are mercilessly sharp, and characters slip in words like “f---wit” and “bonking”, while being aware enough to admit that, well, “No one says ‘bonking’ any more.” Beyond that and the sound design – the Violent Femmes’ Add It Up doesn’t feel appropriate to the general vibe – it’s a faithful, lightly periodised production and an excellent intro to Chekhovian tragicomedy. It’s a rare and charming thing to see Uncle Vanya done in period dress. Pia Johnson Singling out actors for praise in Chekhov may be inevitable but always feels like a betrayal. Star turns can damage the delicate ensemble performance required to portray human contingency and incompleteness, and on that level this production sometimes feels more like a collection of exquisitely rendered individual performances – the human equivalent of the autumn leaves falling in its opening scene – than a true ensemble piece. There’s still much to admire. Sarks emphasises humiliation as key to whatever self-awareness the characters might avoid or achieve, and the romantic excruciations (everyone is famously in love with the wrong person) are beautifully done.

Advertisement

Philippa Northeast invests the role of Sonya with girlish comedy, throwing herself at Astrov (Fayssal Bazzi) with the full cringe of unrequited infatuation, while the charismatic doctor and environmentalist – whose dashing good looks and vaulting idealism coexist with burnout and radical disillusionment and emotional disconnection – seduces the beautiful young Yelena (Catherine Văn-Davies) with a palpable edge of self-loathing. Daniel Henshall’s Vanya is a veritable humiliation magnet. It’s a notably unsympathetic portrayal. A beta male to the core, this Vanya is an intensely pathetic figure who projects his own inadequacies onto his brother-in-law, the Professor (played in a nimble, lightly drawn lampoon of intellectual pomposity by Shaun Micallef) even as he makes embarrassing moves on the Professor’s young wife and pours blatant misogyny over everyone, including his would-be suffragist mother (Carolyn Bock). Daniel Henshall’s Vanya is a veritable humiliation magnet. Pia Johnson Vanya might feel like a minor character in his own life, but it’s Chekhov’s actual minor characters who cope best with humiliation. The longsuffering Waffles (Don Bridges) is warmly and affectionately conveyed, as is the stolidity of the pipe-smoking Nanny (Evelyn Krape). They’re both gloriously unselfconscious – one antidote to humiliation – and such brief moments of freedom are among the production’s most elevating, including a poignant scene where Sonya and Yelena are together, chatting and drinking and playing together like sisters, away from all the fuss the men are causing.

Advertisement

On opening night, some performances didn’t seem entirely bedded down. Henshall appeared to go dry at one point – a metatheatrical humiliation that seemed apposite, in context – but it might be the consistency of dramatic tempo that’s the biggest niggle. Related Article Streaming It may offend the book’s rusted-on fans, but this series should be approached with an open mind How we experience time, and how we handle futility and ennui, are among Chekhov’s main themes, and the one time I saw the Russians perform Vanya – by the Maly Drama Theatre of St Petersburg in 2007 – they brazenly manipulated the elastic temporal quality of theatre. (That production went for over three hours, dared the audience to be bored, and unfolded as inescapably as if it were being performed inside a black hole.) It would be churlish – maybe even Vanya-like – to complain that the audience wasn’t bored enough, though, and if it doesn’t quite deliver the epiphany into the human condition you get from the highest level of Chekhovian performance, this production’s desire to entertain is a no less crucial element of the drama. After all, Chekhov’s characters are always performing to allay such tedium, or at least give it form. And that aspect of being human is as timeless as it gets.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead

Advertisement

MUSIC

Silversun Pickups ★★★★

Forum Melbourne, July 28 When Silversun Pickups walk onto the stage at the Forum, they immediately get to work creating an immersive sonic atmosphere. Not a word is spoken until five songs in, when singer Brian Aubert finally addresses the crowd. Silversun Pickups perform at Forum Melbourne, July 28, 2026. Richard Clifford “Long time no see,” he says. “Since we were last in Melbourne [in 2012], the world fixed itself.” The audience titters. “Just kidding,” Aubert continues, smiling wryly. “It’s all f---ed up, [but] that’s outside these walls … Whatever ectoplasm and debris you’ve been coated in from our so-called leaders, in here, do your best to shake that shit off the best you can.” Indeed, the show is a sensory escape. The Los Angeles rock band’s ’90s-inspired soundscapes, incorporating elements of dream-pop, shoegaze and grunge, come to life on stage, accompanied by dappled lights swirling on the venue’s grand facade. From Aubert’s opening vocals on New Wave, the intensity grows, culminating in Nikki Monninger’s undulating bass, Christopher Guanlao’s thrashing drums and Joe Lester’s keys, collectively so heavy that the floor shakes and vibrates.

Advertisement

The band’s seventh album, Tenterhooks, was released in February, but there were a few more released in the years since they last graced our shores. Still, the bulk of the set is drawn from the new record and fan favourites Carnavas (2006) and Swoon (2009), with only a smattering of songs from the intervening years. After 25 years together, the band is a well-oiled machine, most evident on evocative tracks such as Three Seed, which showcase their ability to build an all-encompassing wall of sound. Nikki Monninger is magnetic as a bassist Richard Clifford Aubert’s distinctive voice has lost none of its sheen. Self-effacing, he jokes about how fans showed up to the now-defunct Ding Dong Lounge for the band’s debut Melbourne headliner in 2007 to see “that girl who sings”. “Surprise,” he deadpans, before performing early track Kissing Families. Monninger and Aubert sing together effortlessly on Panic Switch, but when she takes the lead for Au Revoir Reservoir, her vocals struggle to stay on-key. There’s less power in these moments, but Monninger is magnetic as a bassist, moving with ease and passion as she drives the songs forward. There are few bells and whistles at a Silversun Pickups show – it’s all about losing yourself in the sound, forgetting that anything and everything else exists for a little while. As Aubert sings on the band’s dreamlike signature track Lazy Eye, which closes the night, “It’s the room, the sun and the sky.”

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen

Advertisement

MUSIC

From Winter’s Stillness ★★★★

Australian Chamber Orchestra, Hamer Hall, until July 27 What do you get when you cross the Australian Chamber Orchestra with a jazz trumpeter and a Norwegian trio of female voices specialising in medieval, Nordic folk and contemporary music? Trumpeter Arve Henriksen performs is performing with the Australian Chamber Orchestra. Julia Marie Naglestad Well, certainly an edgy musical hybrid pushing the boundaries of “classical” programming, delighting intrepid listeners and probably perplexing others. The perplexity was heightened because printed programs only became available at interval, leaving most of the audience adrift in the unusual musical terrain of the first half. Trumpeter Arve Henriksen’s The Plume of Ash and Acceptance set a reflective mood, contrasted by the indefatigable minimalism of Terry Riley’s Half Wolf Dances Mad in the Moonlight.

Estonian composer Tõnu Kõrvits’ Bells, written for Henriksen and Trio Mediæval (singers Anna Maria Friman, Ditte Marie Bræin and Jorunn Lovise Husan), exerted a mesmeric quality that sat well alongside Academy Award-winning Icelandic composer Hildur Guðnadóttir’s Time and Water (especially written for this tour). It was worth the wait This Little Child, a sad traditional Norwegian song preceded Icelandic band Sigur Ros’ Fljótavik, an ideal vehicle for Hendriksen, whose unique, mellow tone unfurled over the music’s ground bass. In the second half, movements of Soviet composer Alfred Schnittke’s Concerto Grosso No.1 were interleaved with jazz-infused musings on Nordic chant and folk material. Schnittke’s iconoclasm is mercifully leavened with a generous sense of humour. Soloists Richard Tognetti and Satu Vänskä met the outrageous technical demands with aplomb, aided by customarily fine support from the rest of the ACO.

Using a cyclorama against which performers were either silhouetted or spotlit, head of lighting Joe Cox created a welcoming, unifying mood across this diverse program. Trio Mediæval’s limpid vocal quality was a delight throughout and together with flashes of brilliance from Henriksen, this eclectic experience was bound to get listeners talking – presumably as the ACO intended.

title: Huge delays as Sydney motorway closed due to emergency safety works
text:
Advertisement

Sydney commuters were hit by hours-long delays after the discovery of a faulty fan inside the M5 tunnel overnight triggered emergency works on Wednesday morning, closing the motorway in the city direction during the peak. Motorway operator Transurban eventually reopened the 25-year-old eastbound tunnel shortly before midday following emergency repairs, avoiding it causing further disruption during the afternoon peak. Traffic came to a standstill on the M5. Nine News Premier Chris Minns said the closure had thrown many people’s commute into chaos, and the roads minister would seek answers from Transurban about its maintenance schedule and the chances of a repeat incident. “I know that’s cold comfort for people that were stuck in traffic this morning. I’m genuinely sorry about that,” Minns said. “It’s not good enough.”

Advertisement

The toll road operator had closed the two-lane tunnel to conduct routine maintenance in the early hours of Wednesday when workers discovered safety problems with a fan inside the tunnel. A decision was made on safety grounds about 4.16am to replace the fan and keep the eastbound lanes shut after 5am, despite the looming morning peak. The ongoing closure caused eastbound traffic to queue back as far as 13 kilometres to Milperra during the morning. Two cranes and other equipment were called in for workers to replace the fan, which is one of 147 in the eastbound tunnel. Transurban’s general manager for WestConnex, Denise Kelly, said workers discovered that the fan was faulty during the routine inspection overnight.

Advertisement

“We evaluated it to see whether or not it could be fixed in situ while it stayed up in the roof cavity. That was decided not to be the best course of action, and the best course of action was actually to remove it,” she said. She texted Roads Minister Jenny Aitchison about 4.42am to inform her of the decision to replace the fan and keep the tunnel closed, and the pair later spoke. Kelly confirmed that Transurban was aware at the time of its decision that the tunnel would have to remain closed during the morning peak. “That was the immediate advice to the minister and to the traffic management centre ... that it would be closed for the morning peak,” she said. “We made that call very early, adjusted all of the signs and messaging, and put messaging out on links.”

She apologised to motorists for the major delays caused by the closure, but said that safety had to be prioritised. Transurban is still assessing what caused the faulty fan. title: Inflation fall to pre-Iran war level a welcome surprise
text:
An unexpected drop in headline inflation has eased fears of another imminent interest rate hike.

The latest Australian Bureau of Statistics data showed headline inflation falling from four per cent to 3.8 per cent in June, the lowest level since the outbreak of the US-Iran war in February.

Trimmed mean inflation, the preferred measure by the RBA, remained steady at 3.6 per cent, defying central bank predictions of a rise to 3.8 per cent.

Headline inflation has fallen to the lowest level since the outbreak of the US-Iran war in February. (Susie Dodds/AAP PHOTOS)

The fall in inflation coincided with transport costs moderating for the month, ABS head of price statistics Rachel McCrick said.

"Lower world oil prices as a result of some stabilisation in the Middle East in June contributed to fuel prices falling 10.9 per cent in the month," she said on Wednesday.

"The federal government's fuel excise relief measures, which contributed to lower automatic fuel prices in April and May, also remained in place."

The fuel excise measures reduced the cost of fuel by 32 cents a litre during the month.

However, the measure was reduced to just 16 cents in July, and will be phased out entirely from Sunday.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the inflation figures were reassuring following a period of economic volatility.

"It's an encouraging outcome that shows we've made progress on inflation since the budget, even in the face of intense global uncertainty," he said.

"Treasury has warned that the next phase of the conflict could be more challenging for the global economy, with the oil market now more vulnerable."

The fresh inflation data reduces the chances of another Reserve Bank rate hike in August. (Lukas Coch/AAP PHOTOS)

Quarterly inflation numbers showed headline inflation falling from four to 3.9 per cent.

Meanwhile, the trimmed mean rose from 3.5 per cent in the March quarter to 3.6 per cent in the June quarter.

Housing remained the biggest contributor to inflation for the monthly figures in June, rising by 6.8 per cent.

"Annual inflation for new dwellings has reached its highest level in almost three years, at 5.8 per cent," Ms McCrick said.

"This was driven by builders passing on higher material and labour costs."

The head of economic research at Oxford Economics Australia, Harry Murphy Cruise, said the RBA would be focused less on the headline figures and more on the breadth of price rises.

"Underlying inflation is not just resisting pressure to rise. In quarterly terms, it is continuing to ease," he said.

"All that backs up our view that the RBA will keep rates on hold next month."

The Reserve Bank is due to meet on August 10 and 11 to decide whether interest rates will rise from current levels of 4.35 per cent, or keep them on hold.
